conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What is the key reticulocyte discriminator between sequestration and aplastic crisis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Reticulocytes are HIGH in sequestration (marrow compensating) but LOW in aplastic crisis (marrow suppressed by parvovirus B19) — classic SBA.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: Vaso-occlusive (painful) crisis: mechanism, key discriminator, and management?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Mechanism: capillary occlusion → ischaemia. Discriminator: pain ± fever; dactylitis in children; clinical diagnosis. Management: opioid analgesia, warmth, hydration, O₂; avoid NSAIDs if renal impairment.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: Splenic sequestration crisis: mechanism, key discriminator, and management?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Mechanism: RBC pooling in spleen. Discriminator: enlarged painful spleen + shock; raised reticulocytes. Management: IV fluids + transfusion; splenectomy if recurrent.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: Aplastic crisis: mechanism, key discriminator, and management?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Mechanism: marrow shutdown — parvovirus B19. Discriminator: severe anaemia + low reticulocytes. Management: supportive ± transfusion; self-limiting ~1 week.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: Acute chest syndrome: mechanism, key discriminator, and management?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Mechanism: pulmonary vaso-occlusion/infarct. Discriminator: fever + respiratory symptoms + new CXR infiltrate — leading cause of death. Management: antibiotics, exchange transfusion, analgesia, incentive spirometry, ± NIV.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What is the transfusion logic in sickle cell disease (simple vs exchange)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Simple transfusion for anaemia. Exchange transfusion (rapid HbS% reduction) for stroke, ACS, multiorgan failure, or severe sequestration.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What are the ongoing chronic therapies in sickle cell disease?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Avoid triggers (dehydration, cold, hypoxia, infection); folic acid; hydroxycarbamide (first-line disease-modifier, raises HbF); transfusion for severe anaemia; and — potentially curative — allogeneic stem cell transplant or CRISPR gene therapy (exagamglogene autotemcel / Casgevy).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: Which triggers should be avoided in sickle cell disease?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Dehydration, cold, hypoxia, and infection.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: How does hydroxycarbamide work in sickle cell disease?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: It raises HbF → dilutes HbS → fewer crises; it is the first-line disease-modifying agent.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What are the potentially curative options in sickle cell disease?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Allogeneic stem cell transplant, and — newer — CRISPR gene therapy: exagamglogene autotemcel (Casgevy), MHRA-approved 2023 for severe disease, which edits BCL11A to reactivate HbF.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What is the newer gene therapy for sickle cell disease (and what happened to crizanlizumab/voxelotor)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Exagamglogene autotemcel (Casgevy) — a CRISPR therapy editing BCL11A to raise HbF (MHRA-approved 2023, world-first), potentially curative for severe disease. Crizanlizumab (anti-P-selectin) was withdrawn in 2023 and voxelotor (anti-sickling) worldwide in 2024 — no longer used.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What infection prophylaxis is given for functional asplenia in sickle cell disease?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Penicillin V 500 mg daily (lifelong); pneumococcal vaccine every 5 years; meningococcal, Hib, and annual flu vaccines.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What is the rationale for infection prophylaxis in sickle cell disease?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Recurrent splenic infarction → functional asplenia → encapsulated organism risk (Strep. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, N. meningitidis).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What are the complications on the haemolysis branch?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Chronic anaemia, pigment gallstones, folate deficiency, and aplastic crisis (parvovirus B19).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What are the complications on the vaso-occlusion branch?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Stroke (children), avascular necrosis (hip, shoulder), acute chest syndrome, priapism, CKD/papillary necrosis, pulmonary hypertension, and retinopathy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What are the features of the hyposplenism branch?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Functional asplenia, Howell-Jolly bodies on film, encapsulated organism sepsis — this drives the prophylaxis strategy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the commonest cause of death in sickle cell disease?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Acute chest syndrome — new CXR infiltrate + fever/respiratory symptoms. Needs exchange transfusion.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: EXAM PEARL: Why does functional asplenia produce Howell-Jolly bodies and drive prophylaxis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Functional asplenia → Howell-Jolly bodies on film → lifelong penicillin V + pneumococcal/Hib/meningococcal vaccines.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: EXAM PEARL: Why is exchange (not simple) transfusion used for stroke/ACS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Stroke/ACS need rapid HbS% reduction, so exchange transfusion is used; simple transfusion is for anaemia only.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What is the pathophysiology of a vaso-occlusive (painful) crisis in SCD?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Hypoxia/dehydration/cold/infection → HbS polymerisation → RBC sickling → microvascular occlusion → ischaemia/infarction → severe pain. Most common crisis type.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What is the acute chest syndrome (ACS) in SCD and why is it dangerous?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: New infiltrate on CXR + respiratory symptoms (fever, chest pain, hypoxia) in SCD — fat embolism, infection, or in-situ sickling in pulmonary vasculature. Can be rapidly fatal. Treat: O2, analgesia, exchange transfusion, antibiotics.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What is the role of hydroxyurea (hydroxycarbamide) in SCD?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Increases HbF (foetal haemoglobin) production → dilutes HbS → reduces sickling. Decreases crisis frequency by ~50%. First-line disease-modifying therapy in SCD.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: What vaccinations are mandatory in SCD (asplenic patient)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: Pneumococcal (PCV13 + PPV23), Haemophilus influenzae type b, meningococcal (ACWY + B), annual influenza. Plus prophylactic penicillin V lifelong (or amoxicillin) from infancy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the key electrophoresis finding that distinguishes SCD from sickle cell trait?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Sickle Cell Dis.back: SCD: HbS >90%, HbA absent (only HbS + HbF). Trait (HbAS): HbA ~55–60%, HbS ~40%. Trait patients are carriers — asymptomatic, protected against malaria.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What is the decisive fork in thalassaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Which globin chain, and how many genes are affected? Alpha is graded by number of defective alleles (1→4); beta by trait vs non-transfusion-dependent vs transfusion-dependent. Everything — severity, presentation, transfusion-dependence — falls out of gene dosage.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: How does the Anaemia note cross-reference thalassaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Thalassaemia is a key microcytic cause.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What type of condition is thalassaemia and how is it inherited?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: A haemoglobinopathy — autosomal recessive — with reduced or absent globin chain production.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: Which chromosomes carry the alpha and beta globin defects?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Alpha (chromosome 16) or beta (chromosome 11).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What is the disease mechanism of thalassaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Reduced production of one chain → excess of the paired chain → unstable precipitates → ineffective erythropoiesis + haemolysis → fragile RBCs → splenomegaly. It is the imbalance that causes disease.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What is the mechanism specific to beta-thalassaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Chromosome 11 mutation → reduced/absent beta chain → excess alpha chains precipitate → haemolysis + ineffective erythropoiesis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: Beta-thalassaemia trait (carrier): genotype, symptoms, Hb, and key features?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Genotype: heterozygous (β/β⁺ or β/β⁰). Symptoms: asymptomatic. Hb: mildly low or normal. Key features: low MCV, low MCH; disproportionate microcytosis; normal ferritin.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: Non-transfusion-dependent beta-thalassaemia: genotype, symptoms, Hb, and key features?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Genotype: intermediate. Symptoms: moderate anaemia. Hb: 70–100 g/L. Key features: splenomegaly, bone deformities, leg ulcers, gallstones.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: Transfusion-dependent beta-thalassaemia (major): genotype, symptoms, Hb, and key features?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Genotype: homozygous (β⁰/β⁰). Symptoms: severe — presents in the first year of life. Hb: severely low. Key features: failure to thrive, recurrent infection, hepatosplenomegaly, bony changes.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What is the highest-yield trait vs IDA discriminator in thalassaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: In thalassaemia trait, ferritin and iron stores are normal, and the microcytosis is disproportionate to the degree of anaemia. IDA has low ferritin, raised TIBC, low iron. HbA2 >3.5% on electrophoresis confirms beta-thalassaemia trait.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What bony abnormalities occur in thalassaemia and why?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Marrow expansion from extramedullary haemopoiesis → hepatosplenomegaly; raised fracture risk, enlarged maxilla, frontal/parietal bossing; 'hair-on-end' skull X-ray appearance.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What causes the bony deformities and hepatosplenomegaly in thalassaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Extramedullary haemopoiesis → hepatosplenomegaly; marrow expansion → raised fracture risk, enlarged maxilla, frontal/parietal bossing.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What is the classic skull X-ray finding in thalassaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: 'Hair-on-end' appearance.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What is the genetic basis of alpha-thalassaemia, and what forms the unstable tetramers?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Chromosome 16; 4 alpha-globin genes. Severity is determined by the number of defective alleles. Excess gamma chains (fetal) or beta chains form unstable tetramers (HbH, Hb Barts).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: Alpha-thalassaemia with 1 allele affected: name and clinical picture?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Minima (silent carrier) — asymptomatic; normal MCV.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: Alpha-thalassaemia with 2 alleles affected: name and clinical picture?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Trait — asymptomatic; mild low MCV.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: Alpha-thalassaemia with 3 alleles affected: name and clinical picture?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: HbH disease — mild–severe haemolytic anaemia; jaundice, gallstones, splenomegaly, leg ulcers, osteopenia, ± aplastic crises.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: Alpha-thalassaemia with 4 alleles affected: name and clinical picture?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Hb Barts — hydrops fetalis, incompatible with life; stillborn.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: Why does alpha-thalassaemia trait need genetic testing to diagnose?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Alpha thalassaemia trait often has a normal Hb electrophoresis — diagnosis requires genetic testing (or HPLC showing Hb Barts in neonates).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What does the FBC + film show in thalassaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Hypochromic microcytic anaemia; raised reticulocytes; nucleated RBCs in the periphery; target cells.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What does Hb electrophoresis / HPLC show in beta major vs beta trait?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Beta major: raised HbF, absent/reduced HbA. Beta trait: raised HbA2 (>3.5%).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What do ferritin / iron studies show in thalassaemia trait, and why does it matter?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Normal in trait — which distinguishes it from IDA.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: Which investigation is required for alpha-thalassaemia, and why?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Genetic testing — because the electrophoresis may be normal.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What antenatal and ongoing monitoring is offered in thalassaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Antenatal screening — a haemoglobinopathy screen offered at booking. Serum ferritin (ongoing) — monitoring for transfusional iron overload.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: How is transfusion-dependent (major) thalassaemia managed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Regular transfusions to keep Hb >100 g/L (suppresses ineffective erythropoiesis, prevents bony deformity); lifelong folic acid; splenectomy for hypersplenism (vaccinate first: pneumococcal, meningococcal, Hib + prophylactic penicillin V); and — potentially curative — allogeneic stem cell transplant or CRISPR gene therapy (exagamglogene autotemcel / Casgevy).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: Why are regular transfusions given in thalassaemia major?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: To keep Hb >100 g/L — this suppresses ineffective erythropoiesis and prevents bony deformity.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What must be done before splenectomy in thalassaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Vaccinate first (pneumococcal, meningococcal, Hib) and give prophylactic penicillin V.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What are the potentially curative options in thalassaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Allogeneic stem cell transplant, and — newer — CRISPR gene therapy: exagamglogene autotemcel (Casgevy), MHRA-approved 2023 for transfusion-dependent β-thalassaemia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: How is trait / mild thalassaemia managed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: No treatment required; genetic counselling; avoid unnecessary iron supplementation.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: Why is iron overload the central long-term problem in thalassaemia, and which organs are affected?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Transfusional iron accumulates in organs: heart → cardiomyopathy/cardiac failure (leading cause of death); liver → cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma; pituitary → growth failure, infertility; thyroid/parathyroid → hypothyroidism, hypoparathyroidism; pancreas → diabetes mellitus; gonads → hypogonadism, delayed puberty.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What is the leading cause of death in thalassaemia major, and how is iron overload treated?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Cardiac iron overload (cardiomyopathy/cardiac failure) is the leading cause of death. Iron chelation: subcutaneous desferrioxamine or oral deferasirox/deferiprone. Monitor serum ferritin.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: EXAM PEARL: How do you tell thalassaemia trait from IDA, and what confirms beta trait?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Disproportionate microcytosis + normal ferritin → think thalassaemia trait, not IDA. HbA2 >3.5% confirms beta-thalassaemia trait on electrophoresis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: EXAM PEARL: What do Hb Barts (4 alleles) and HbH (3 alleles) represent?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Hb Barts (4 alleles) = hydrops fetalis, incompatible with life. HbH (3 alleles) = symptomatic but survivable haemolytic anaemia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: EXAM PEARL: How does electrophoresis differ between alpha and beta trait?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Alpha thalassaemia trait — electrophoresis can be normal; needs genetic testing. Beta trait — electrophoresis shows raised HbA2.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What is the Hb electrophoresis finding in beta-thalassaemia major?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: HbA absent (no beta chains); HbF elevated (>90%) as main oxygen carrier; HbA2 elevated. Severe microcytic anaemia requiring transfusion from 6 months.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What is beta-thalassaemia intermedia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Intermediate severity — two beta-globin gene mutations but less severe than major. Can maintain Hb 7–10 without regular transfusion. Requires transfusion only periodically or in crises.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What skull radiograph finding is seen in severe beta-thalassaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: 'Hair-on-end' (crew-cut) skull — cortical thinning with vertical striations from marrow expansion trying to compensate for anaemia. Also: 'chipmunk facies' from maxillary hypertrophy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What is the management of beta-thalassaemia major?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Regular transfusions (every 3–4 weeks, target Hb >90–100 g/L pre-transfusion); iron chelation (desferrioxamine SC or deferasirox oral); and — potentially curative — HLA-matched allogeneic SCT or CRISPR gene therapy (exagamglogene autotemcel / Casgevy, MHRA-approved 2023).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: What is Hb H disease and how does it present?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: 3 deleted alpha-globin genes → Hb H (β4 tetramers) — moderately severe haemolytic anaemia. Splenomegaly, Hb ~70–100 g/L, intermittent transfusion. Hb electrophoresis shows HbH.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.front: EXAM PEARL: How does thalassaemia trait differ from iron deficiency on FBC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thalassaemia.back: Both: microcytic hypochromic anaemia. Thalassaemia trait: normal/high red cell count (RCC), normal/low ferritin normal, high HbA2 on electrophoresis. Iron deficiency: low RCC, low ferritin, normal HbA2. Mentzer index: <13 = thalassaemia; >13 = iron deficiency.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What is multiple myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: A malignant clonal proliferation of bone marrow plasma cells → monoclonal paraprotein (usually IgG > IgA).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What is the single dividing line between myeloma and its precursor states?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: End-organ damage: MGUS and smouldering myeloma lack CRAB; myeloma has it. That single discriminator is how the spectrum is examined.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: MGUS: defining feature and presence of end-organ (CRAB) damage?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Incidental paraprotein, <10% plasma cells. No CRAB — monitor annually.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: Smouldering myeloma: defining feature and presence of end-organ (CRAB) damage?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Higher paraprotein / 10–60% plasma cells. No CRAB — premalignant; higher progression risk.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: Multiple myeloma: defining feature and presence of end-organ (CRAB) damage?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Paraprotein + clonal plasma cells. Yes — CRAB present.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What is Waldenström's macroglobulinaemia and how does it present?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: The IgM variant (lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma). Presents with hyperviscosity, not bone disease — a distinct entity.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What are the risk factors for myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Older age, male, Black African ethnicity, family history, obesity.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What does the 'C' in CRAB stand for, with features and mechanism?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: HyperCalcaemia → constipation, nausea, confusion, polyuria, thirst ('bones, groans, moans, stones'). Mechanism: osteoclastic bone resorption driven by myeloma cytokines.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What does the 'R' in CRAB stand for, with mechanism?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Renal failure. Mechanism: light-chain cast nephropathy, hypercalcaemia, hyperuricaemia, amyloid, dehydration, nephrotoxic drugs.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What does the 'A' in CRAB stand for, with mechanism?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Anaemia (normocytic normochromic) ± pancytopenia. Mechanism: marrow infiltration crowds out normal haematopoiesis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What does the 'B' in CRAB stand for, with sites and mechanism?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Bone pain / lytic lesions — skull, spine, ribs, pelvis, long bones. Mechanism: IL-1/TNF-α → osteoclast activation → resorption without repair.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What are the features of the paraprotein / hyperviscosity branch in myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Blurred vision, headache; bleeding/bruising (impaired platelet function); infections — immunoparesis (reduced normal polyclonal Ig); peripheral neuropathy; heart failure (hyperviscosity).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: Why do myeloma patients get recurrent infections?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Immunoparesis — reduced normal polyclonal Ig.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What emergency presentation must not be delayed in a myeloma patient with back pain + new neurological signs?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Spinal cord compression — back pain + new neurological signs in a myeloma patient = urgent MRI spine. Do not delay.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: Besides spinal cord compression, what other emergency presentations occur in myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Acute hypercalcaemia, renal failure, hyperviscosity crisis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What is the two-step investigation pathway in myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Initial screen → if suspicious, send BLIP → confirm with bone marrow biopsy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What does the initial screen show in myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: FBC: low Hb, ± pancytopenia; raised ESR, raised plasma viscosity; raised calcium, raised creatinine; raised total protein, low albumin; urine dipstick negative for Bence-Jones (dipstick detects albumin, not light chains).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: Why is the urine dipstick negative for Bence-Jones protein in myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: The dipstick detects albumin, not light chains — so you must send urine electrophoresis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What does the 'B' in the BLIP diagnostic panel stand for?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Urine electrophoresis for Bence-Jones protein (urinary light chains).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What does the 'L' in the BLIP diagnostic panel stand for?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Serum-free light-chain assay.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What does the 'I' in the BLIP diagnostic panel stand for?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Serum immunoglobulins (paraprotein type).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What does the 'P' in the BLIP diagnostic panel stand for?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Serum protein electrophoresis — monoclonal band.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What confirms the diagnosis on bone marrow biopsy in myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Clonal plasma cells ≥10% (or plasmacytoma). Combined with CRAB criteria = diagnostic of myeloma.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What is the imaging preference order in myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: 1. Whole-body MRI — first-line. 2. Whole-body CT. 3. Skeletal survey (plain X-ray).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What are the classic imaging signs in myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Punched-out lytic lesions, raindrop skull, vertebral collapse.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What is the standard first-line anti-myeloma therapy?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: The bortezomib + thalidomide + dexamethasone (VTD) triplet is the backbone; current practice adds daratumumab (anti-CD38) — the "Dara-VTd" quadruplet is now standard first-line for transplant-eligible patients, followed by autologous SCT.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What anti-myeloma therapy is used in fit patients, and what is the disease course?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Autologous stem cell transplant in fit patients. Relapsing-remitting course; managed by haem-onc MDT.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: How is bone disease managed in myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Bisphosphonates (zoledronate) — suppress osteoclasts, reduce fractures; radiotherapy for localised bone pain; orthopaedic stabilisation for pathological fracture; vertebroplasty/kyphoplasty for vertebral collapse.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What is the role of bisphosphonates (zoledronate) in myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: They suppress osteoclasts and reduce fractures.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: VTE PROPHYLAXIS EXAM TRAP: Why must aspirin or LMWH be co-prescribed with thalidomide?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Thalidomide is prothrombotic → must co-prescribe aspirin or LMWH. A classic MCQ distractor.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What supportive care is given in myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: IV hydration + treat hypercalcaemia; transfusion for symptomatic anaemia; infection prophylaxis + vaccinations; renal: avoid NSAIDs/nephrotoxins, dialysis if needed.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What are the complications on the marrow / bone branch in myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Anaemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia; recurrent infections (immunoparesis); pathological fractures; spinal cord compression; hypercalcaemia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: What are the complications on the paraprotein branch in myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Renal failure (cast nephropathy); hyperviscosity syndrome; AL amyloid → cardiac, renal, peripheral neuropathy; treatment-related neuropathy (bortezomib, thalidomide).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: EXAM PEARL: What is CRAB and why does it matter?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: CRAB is the diagnostic tetrad. Its presence separates myeloma from MGUS/smouldering — the single most important discriminator.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: EXAM PEARL: When should you screen for myeloma in an older patient with bone symptoms?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Over-60 + persistent back pain or unexplained fracture → screen for myeloma. Do not attribute to mechanical or osteoporotic causes without checking.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the classic radiology of myeloma, and what is the preferred first-line imaging?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Raindrop skull + punched-out lytic lesions = classic radiology. Whole-body MRI is now first-line imaging (more sensitive than skeletal survey).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: EXAM PEARL: What is Bence-Jones protein, and why is the urine dipstick misleading?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Bence-Jones protein = urinary light chains. The urine dipstick is negative because it detects albumin, not light chains — must send urine electrophoresis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the thalidomide VTE trap?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Thalidomide → VTE — always co-prescribe aspirin or LMWH. A guaranteed MCQ trap.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: EXAM PEARL: How does Waldenström's differ from myeloma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: Waldenström's = IgM variant; hyperviscosity not bone disease. Anaemia is normocytic normochromic; ESR and plasma viscosity raised.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the CRAB criteria for myeloma and what does each letter stand for?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloma.back: C — hypercalcaemia (>2.75 mmol/L); R — renal failure (creatinine >177); A — anaemia (Hb <100 g/L); B — bone lesions (lytic lesions / osteoporosis). One or more = symptomatic myeloma requiring treatment.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What defines Hodgkin lymphoma (HL) — hallmark cell, markers, age, spread, cure rate?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Reed-Sternberg cells present (owl-eye nuclei); CD15+, CD30+ (NOT CD20); bimodal age 20s & 60s; contiguous nodal spread; ~85% cure rate.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What defines Non-Hodgkin lymphoma (NHL) — hallmark cell, origin, age, spread, cure rate?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: No Reed-Sternberg cells; B-cell or T-cell origin; peak age >60; non-contiguous, extranodal spread; variable cure rate (10–90%).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: HL vs NHL: what is the hallmark cell of each?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Hodgkin: Reed-Sternberg (owl-eye nuclei). Non-Hodgkin: lymphocytes (B or T).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: HL vs NHL: how does the age distribution differ?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Hodgkin: bimodal (20s & 60s). Non-Hodgkin: any age, peak >60.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: HL vs NHL: how does the pattern of spread differ?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Hodgkin: contiguous nodal. Non-Hodgkin: non-contiguous, extranodal.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: HL vs NHL: how do B symptoms and mediastinal mass compare?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: B symptoms: common in Hodgkin, less common in Non-Hodgkin. Mediastinal mass: common in Hodgkin, less common in Non-Hodgkin (except DLBCL).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: HL vs NHL: what is the EBV association of each?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Hodgkin: yes (mixed cellularity). Non-Hodgkin: Burkitt's.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: HL vs NHL: how do cure rates compare?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Hodgkin: ~85%. Non-Hodgkin: variable (10–90%).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What are the risk factors for Hodgkin lymphoma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: EBV (especially mixed cellularity subtype), HIV, immunosuppression.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: How does Hodgkin lymphoma present?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Painless cervical lymphadenopathy; mediastinal mass on CXR; B symptoms (fever >38°C, drenching night sweats, >10% weight loss in 6 months); buzzword: alcohol-induced nodal pain — pathognomonic for HL.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What is the pathognomonic buzzword for Hodgkin lymphoma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Alcohol-induced nodal pain.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What are the B symptoms in lymphoma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Fever >38°C, drenching night sweats, >10% weight loss in 6 months.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What investigations are used in Hodgkin lymphoma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Excision biopsy → Reed-Sternberg cells (CD15+, CD30+, owl-eye nuclei); PET-CT for staging; FBC: eosinophilia, lymphopenia in advanced disease; ESR: disease activity marker.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What is the first-line chemotherapy regimen for Hodgkin lymphoma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: ABVD chemotherapy ± radiotherapy: Adriamycin (doxorubicin), Bleomycin, Vinblastine, Dacarbazine.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What does ABVD stand for in Hodgkin lymphoma management?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Adriamycin (doxorubicin), Bleomycin, Vinblastine, Dacarbazine.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What is the key toxicity of bleomycin in ABVD?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Pulmonary fibrosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What is the key toxicity of adriamycin (doxorubicin) in ABVD?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Cardiomyopathy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What is the key toxicity of vinblastine in ABVD?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Peripheral neuropathy, constipation.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What are the general features of Non-Hodgkin lymphoma and its standard chemotherapy?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: More common than HL; most are B-cell origin; managed with R-CHOP (Rituximab + Cyclophosphamide + Hydroxydaunorubicin/doxorubicin + Oncovin/vincristine + Prednisolone).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What does R-CHOP stand for in NHL management?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Rituximab, Cyclophosphamide, Hydroxydaunorubicin/doxorubicin, Oncovin/vincristine, Prednisolone.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: DLBCL: key features and translocation/marker?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Diffuse Large B-Cell — most common NHL, aggressive, potentially curable. t(14;18) in some; BCL-2.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: Follicular lymphoma: key features and translocation/marker?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Indolent, incurable but manageable; 'waxing and waning' lymph nodes. t(14;18); BCL-2 overexpression.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: Burkitt's lymphoma: key features and translocation/marker?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Highly aggressive; 'starry sky' histology; jaw mass (African endemic). EBV association: endemic (African) form is EBV-driven (+ malaria co-factor); sporadic and HIV-associated forms are usually EBV-negative. t(8;14); MYC.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: MALT lymphoma: key features and management point?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Gastric; associated with H. pylori — treat H. pylori first.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: Mantle cell lymphoma: key features and translocation/marker?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Aggressive, poor prognosis. t(11;14); cyclin D1.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What is tumour lysis syndrome and its biochemical picture?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Massive cell death after chemo → raised K⁺, raised phosphate, low Ca²⁺, raised uric acid → renal failure, arrhythmia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: How is tumour lysis syndrome prevented?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: IV fluids + allopurinol or rasburicase before chemotherapy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: Ann Arbor staging: what are stages I and II?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: I: single nodal region. II: ≥2 nodal regions, same side of diaphragm.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: Ann Arbor staging: what are stages III and IV?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: III: nodal regions on both sides of the diaphragm. IV: extranodal spread (liver, bone marrow).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What do the A and B suffixes mean in Ann Arbor staging?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: A = no B symptoms. B = B symptoms present (fever >38°C, drenching night sweats, >10% weight loss in 6 months).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the marker profile of Reed-Sternberg cells?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: RS cells are CD15+ and CD30+ — NOT CD20.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: EXAM PEARL: What symptom is pathognomonic for Hodgkin lymphoma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Alcohol-induced nodal pain.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: EXAM PEARL: What are the key chemotherapy toxicities to remember (bleomycin, doxorubicin)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Bleomycin → pulmonary fibrosis; doxorubicin → cardiomyopathy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: EXAM PEARL: What are the translocations for Burkitt's and follicular lymphoma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Burkitt's = t(8;14) MYC; follicular = t(14;18) BCL-2.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: EXAM PEARL: How does H. pylori eradication relate to MALT lymphoma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: H. pylori eradication can cure early gastric MALT lymphoma.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the tumour lysis biochemistry and how is it prevented?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Tumour lysis: raised K, raised PO₄, low Ca, raised uric acid — prevent with hydration + allopurinol.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What is the Ann Arbor staging system for lymphoma?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Stage I: single nodal region; Stage II: ≥2 regions same side of diaphragm; Stage III: both sides of diaphragm; Stage IV: extranodal involvement. Add A (no B symptoms) or B (fever >38°C, night sweats, weight loss >10%).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What are the B symptoms in lymphoma and their significance?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: Fever >38°C, drenching night sweats, weight loss >10% in 6 months — indicate systemic disease (stage B), worse prognosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: What is the International Prognostic Index (IPI) for DLBCL?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: 5 factors: age >60, stage III/IV, raised LDH, ECOG performance status ≥2, >1 extranodal site. Each = 1 point: 0–1 low risk; 4–5 high risk.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.front: EXAM PEARL: What differentiates Hodgkin from non-Hodgkin lymphoma clinically?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Lymphoma.back: HL: young adults, contiguous spread, mediastinal mass, Reed-Sternberg cells, highly curable (>80%). NHL: older, non-contiguous, extranodal common, diverse subtypes, variable prognosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What is leukaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: A malignancy of haematopoietic stem cells → marrow replaced by clonal cells → other lineages suppressed (anaemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What is the two-axis classification of leukaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Speed (Acute/Chronic) × Lineage (Myeloid/Lymphoid).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: How do lymphoma and leukaemia differ in what they affect (cross-reference)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Lymphoma affects nodes; leukaemia affects marrow/blood.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: In the 2×2 master grid, what defines acute myeloid leukaemia (AML)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Acute (blasts) + myeloid. >75y; commonest acute leukaemia; Auer rods; raised risk after MDS/myeloproliferative disease.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: In the 2×2 master grid, what defines acute lymphoblastic leukaemia (ALL)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Acute (blasts) + lymphoid. Children (<5) & >45y; Down's syndrome; CNS spread; commonest childhood cancer.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: In the 2×2 master grid, what defines chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Chronic (mature) + myeloid. ~65y; Philadelphia t(9;22)/BCR-ABL; massive splenomegaly; 3 phases.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: In the 2×2 master grid, what defines chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (CLL)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Chronic (mature) + lymphoid. >55y; commonest leukaemia overall; smudge cells; Richter's transformation.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What is the age mnemonic for the four leukaemias?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: ALL <5 & >45 · CLL >55 · CML ~65 · AML >75 (rises across the alphabet).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What are the four key buzzword associations in leukaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Auer rods → AML; Philadelphia t(9;22)/BCR-ABL → CML; smudge cells → CLL; Down's syndrome & CNS spread → ALL.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What is the general aetiology of leukaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Genetic change → clonal population. Triggers: benzene, alkylating agents (→ secondary AML), radiation, HTLV-1, Down's syndrome (30× risk, especially ALL).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What does t(9;22) Philadelphia → BCR-ABL signify and how is it targeted?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Present in >95% CML, and some ALL → target with imatinib (TKI).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What does t(15;17) → PML-RARα signify and how is it targeted?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: APML (AML subtype) → blocks differentiation → target with ATRA.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What is the biochemical picture of tumour lysis syndrome?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Chemo lyses cells → raised urate, raised K⁺, raised phosphate, low Ca²⁺ → AKI (urate crystals).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: How is laboratory tumour lysis syndrome defined?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: ≥2 abnormalities within 3 days pre / 7 days post chemo.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: How is tumour lysis syndrome prevented, and what is the key distinction between the two agents?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Allopurinol (xanthine oxidase inhibitor — prevents urate formation) OR rasburicase (urate oxidase — breaks down existing urate to allantoin) + IV hydration. Never give both together. Key distinction: allopurinol works upstream/preventatively; rasburicase works on already-formed urate.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: Why must allopurinol and rasburicase never be given together?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Allopurinol works upstream/preventatively (prevents urate formation) while rasburicase works on already-formed urate — they are not given together.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: How does acute leukaemia present (marrow failure)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Anaemia (low RBC); bleeding/petechiae (low platelets/thrombocytopenia); infection (low neutrophils/neutropenia); ± lymphadenopathy/hepatosplenomegaly.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What are the differentials for a non-blanching rash (relevant to acute leukaemia)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Leukaemia, meningococcaemia, ITP, HSP, vasculitis, NAI.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What investigations are used in acute leukaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: FBC: low Hb, low platelets, WCC raised or low; bone marrow aspirate + film = definitive; Auer rods = AML (pathognomonic); immunophenotyping for lineage; LP in ALL (CNS risk); MRD by flow cytometry guides relapse risk and de-escalation.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What is the definitive investigation in acute leukaemia, and what confirms AML on it?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Bone marrow aspirate + film is definitive; Auer rods are pathognomonic for AML.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What does MRD by flow cytometry guide in acute leukaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Relapse risk and de-escalation.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: AML: age, hallmark, risk factor, and chemo?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Age predominantly >75y; hallmark Auer rods (pathognomonic); raised risk after MDS or myeloproliferative disease; chemo cytarabine + daunorubicin; transplant for intermediate/high-risk.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What is the APML subtype of AML, its association, and treatment?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: APML (~25y): t(15;17), associated with DIC (can worsen on treatment) → ATRA reverses bleeding and drives differentiation.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: ALL: age, associations, CNS management, and significance?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Age children (<5y) and >45y; associations Down's syndrome and ionising radiation; CNS spread → LP + intrathecal methotrexate; commonest childhood cancer. (EBV is linked to Burkitt/mature B-ALL, not typical ALL.)

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What is the ALL chemotherapy and maintenance?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Vincristine, dexamethasone, asparaginase, daunorubicin; 2-year maintenance.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: How is Philadelphia+ ALL and B-ALL managed beyond standard chemo?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Philadelphia+ ALL: add TKI (imatinib). B-ALL monoclonals: rituximab (anti-CD20), blinatumomab (CD19/CD3).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: CML key facts: genetics, age, and the three phases?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Philadelphia chromosome t(9;22) → BCR-ABL in >95%; age ~65, middle-aged; three phases: Chronic (~5 years, often incidental raised WCC) → Accelerated → Blast crisis (>30% blasts, usually transforms to AML, often fatal).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: How does CML present?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Insidious onset: fever, weight loss, sweats; massive splenomegaly; blood film: leucocytosis with myeloid precursors, basophilia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: How is CML managed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Imatinib (TKI — blocks BCR-ABL): first-line; allogeneic SCT / interferon for advanced disease.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: CLL key facts: frequency, age/cells, blood film, and immunophenotype?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Commonest leukaemia overall; elderly patients (>55y); clonal mature B-cells; indolent but incurable; blood film smudge/smear cells; immunophenotype CD5, CD19, CD20, CD23.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What is the immunophenotype of CLL?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: CD5, CD19, CD20, CD23.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: How does CLL present and what are its key complications?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Often asymptomatic — incidental lymphocytosis on routine bloods; later marrow failure features, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly; AIHA (warm antibody); Richter's transformation → high-grade lymphoma (DLBCL).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What is Richter's transformation in CLL?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Transformation to a high-grade lymphoma (DLBCL).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: How is CLL managed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Watch-and-wait (early/asymptomatic disease); symptomatic/progressive: FCR (fludarabine, cyclophosphamide, rituximab) — now largely second-line; modern first-line: BTK inhibitors (ibrutinib/acalabrutinib) or venetoclax ± obinutuzumab.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: What is the modern first-line treatment for CLL?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: BTK inhibitors (ibrutinib/acalabrutinib) or venetoclax ± obinutuzumab.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: EXAM PEARL: How does the 2×2 capture the whole leukaemia topic?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Acute = blasts/marrow failure/emergency; chronic = mature/insidious/incidental.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: EXAM PEARL: Summarise the four buzzword associations.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Auer rods → AML; Philadelphia/BCR-ABL → CML; smudge cells → CLL; Down's & CNS → ALL.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: EXAM PEARL: What do imatinib and ATRA target?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: Imatinib (TKI) targets BCR-ABL in CML/Ph+ ALL; ATRA targets PML-RARα in APML.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the classic APML vignette?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: APML → DIC (can worsen on chemo) — the classic vignette; cross-reference the DIC note.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: EXAM PEARL: What two transformations/complications are linked to CLL?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: CLL → Richter's transformation (DLBCL) and AIHA.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.front: EXAM PEARL: Contrast allopurinol and rasburicase, and state the two 'commonest' facts.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Leukaemia (acut.back: TLS: allopurinol (prevents urate) vs rasburicase (breaks down urate) — never both. ALL = commonest childhood cancer; CLL = commonest leukaemia overall.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What are myeloproliferative disorders (MPDs)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: Uncontrolled clonal proliferation of a single myeloid stem cell line — cells are still mature (contrast acute leukaemia, where blasts fail to differentiate).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What is the unifying genetics of MPDs and what can they all transform to?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: JAK2 (also MPL, CALR mutations). All can transform to AML.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What are the three classical types of MPD and their proliferating lines?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: PV — erythroid line raised; ET — megakaryocyte line raised; primary myelofibrosis — HSC → marrow fibrosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: How does CML relate to the MPDs (cross-reference)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: CML is the 4th classical MPD but uses BCR-ABL, not JAK2 — the key discriminator.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What is the exam SBA fork in approaching polycythaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: 'Is this even true polycythaemia?'

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: Absolute polycythaemia: what defines it, and what are the primary and secondary subtypes with EPO levels?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: Absolute = true raised red cell mass. Primary = PV (JAK2 mutation, marrow-driven; EPO LOW). Secondary = chronic hypoxia (lung disease, high altitude, R→L shunt, heavy smoking) or EPO-secreting tumour (renal, hepatic, cerebellar); EPO HIGH.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: Relative/apparent polycythaemia: what defines it and its two causes?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: Normal red cell mass with low plasma volume. Gaisböck syndrome — middle-aged obese men, smoking, HTN, alcohol (EPO normal); dehydration — simple volume depletion (EPO normal).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What is the key discriminator that separates dangerous clonal polycythaemia from reactive causes?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: EPO is LOW in PV (marrow autonomy suppresses EPO) but HIGH in secondary polycythaemia — this single value separates the dangerous clonal disease from reactive causes.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: MPD discriminator: what is the proliferating line in PV vs ET vs MF?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: PV: raised RBC (± plt, neut). ET: raised platelets. MF: marrow fibrosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: MPD discriminator: what proportion are JAK2-positive in PV vs ET vs MF?
MPD discriminator: what is the hallmark of PV vs ET vs MF?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: PV: aquagenic pruritus, ruddy plethora, raised Hct. ET: thrombosis ± bleeding. MF: massive splenomegaly.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: MPD discriminator: what is the blood film clue in PV vs ET vs MF?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: PV: raised haematocrit. ET: abnormal large platelets. MF: teardrop poikilocytes, leucoerythroblastic.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: MPD discriminator: what does the bone marrow show in PV vs ET vs MF?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: PV: hypercellular. ET: raised megakaryocytes. MF: dry tap → trephine.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: MPD discriminator: what is the 1st-line treatment in PV vs ET vs MF?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: PV: venesection (PCV <0.45) + aspirin. ET: aspirin + cytoreduction. MF: supportive; ruxolitinib; BMT (only cure).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What are the features of polycythaemia vera (PV)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: Aquagenic pruritus after a hot bath (the hallmark); conjunctival plethora, ruddy complexion, hypertension; hyperviscosity → thrombosis (stroke, DVT, Budd-Chiari); haemorrhage (abnormal platelet function); headache, visual disturbance, gout, angina.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What is the hallmark feature of polycythaemia vera?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: Aquagenic pruritus after a hot bath.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What are the investigation findings in polycythaemia vera?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: Raised haematocrit; JAK2+ with raised Hct = confirmed; low ESR (high viscosity paradox); low EPO (separates from secondary polycythaemia).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What confirms a diagnosis of polycythaemia vera?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: JAK2+ with a raised haematocrit.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: How is polycythaemia vera managed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: Venesection (PCV <0.45) — first-line; aspirin (antithrombotic); cytoreduction with hydroxycarbamide, busulfan, α-interferon; anagrelide for thrombocytosis; ruxolitinib (JAK2 inhibitor).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What is the first-line management of polycythaemia vera?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: Venesection (PCV <0.45).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What is the pathophysiology of myelofibrosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: Stem cell proliferation → abnormal megakaryocytes release PDGF → fibroblast activation → marrow fibrosis. Can arise de novo (primary) or evolve from PV/ET.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What are the features of myelofibrosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: Anaemia (fatigue — commonest symptom); bleeding; hypermetabolic: weight loss, night sweats; massive hepatosplenomegaly → portal hypertension (extramedullary haemopoiesis).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What is the commonest symptom of myelofibrosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: Fatigue (from anaemia).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What causes the massive hepatosplenomegaly in myelofibrosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: Extramedullary haemopoiesis → massive hepatosplenomegaly → portal hypertension.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What are the investigation findings in myelofibrosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: Anaemia; WCC/platelets high early, fall late; film: leucoerythroblastic + teardrop poikilocytes; raised urate, raised LDH; dry tap → trephine biopsy (the classic pairing).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What is the classic blood film + biopsy pairing in myelofibrosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: Leucoerythroblastic + teardrop poikilocytes on film, with a dry tap → trephine biopsy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: How is myelofibrosis managed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: Transfusions, allopurinol, ruxolitinib (JAK2 inhibitor). Allogeneic BMT = only cure.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What are the features of essential thrombocythaemia (ET)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: Normal Hb + normal WCC, isolated raised platelets. Platelets abnormal in size/function → thrombosis > bleeding. Diagnosis of exclusion — rule out reactive thrombocytosis (infection, iron deficiency, malignancy) first.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: Why is essential thrombocythaemia a diagnosis of exclusion?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: You must rule out reactive thrombocytosis (infection, iron deficiency, malignancy) first.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: How is essential thrombocythaemia managed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: Aspirin in all patients. Cytoreduction if high-risk: hydroxycarbamide, anagrelide, busulfan, interferon.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: EXAM PEARL: What does aquagenic pruritus after a hot bath indicate?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: PV until proven otherwise.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: EXAM PEARL: How does EPO distinguish PV from secondary polycythaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: EPO is low in PV (marrow autonomy); EPO is high in secondary polycythaemia — the key discriminator.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the signature pairing for myelofibrosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: Teardrop poikilocytes + dry tap = myelofibrosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: EXAM PEARL: Summarise the JAK2 positivity rates and the CML discriminator.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: JAK2: ~95% PV, ~50% ET/MF. CML uses BCR-ABL — not JAK2.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: EXAM PEARL: What are the treatment backbones for PV and ET?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: Venesection + aspirin = PV backbone; aspirin alone = ET backbone.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: EXAM PEARL: Summarise the transformation/end-stage and key category points across MPDs.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: All MPDs can transform to AML; myelofibrosis can be the end-stage of PV/ET. ET = diagnosis of exclusion; Gaisböck = relative (apparent) polycythaemia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What is the JAK2 V617F mutation and which MPDs carry it?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: Point mutation in Janus kinase 2 → constitutive cytokine signalling. PV: 95%; ET: 50–60%; MF: 50–60%. Absent in CML (which has BCR-ABL instead).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What is myelofibrosis and its classic blood film finding?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: MPD → progressive marrow fibrosis (reticulin/collagen) → extramedullary haematopoiesis (splenomegaly). Film: leukoerythroblastic picture + teardrop poikilocytes (dacrocytes) — classic 'tear drop cells'.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: What is the treatment target in polycythaemia vera (venesection target)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: Target haematocrit <0.45 in males, <0.42 in females. Aspirin 75 mg daily for all PV. Hydroxycarbamide for high-risk cytoreduction.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the Budd-Chiari syndrome association with MPDs?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myeloproliferat.back: JAK2 V617F mutation causes thrombophilia → Budd-Chiari (hepatic vein thrombosis) and portal vein thrombosis. Test for JAK2 in any young patient with unprovoked mesenteric or hepatic vein thrombosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What is the defining paradox of myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Hypercellular marrow + peripheral pancytopenia — the clonal cells proliferate but die by premature apoptosis before reaching the blood (marrow is full; periphery is empty).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What is MDS (definition)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: A group of acquired clonal bone marrow disorders → ineffective haematopoiesis → progressive marrow failure.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: Where does MDS sit on the disease spectrum?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Cytopenias → MDS → AML. MDS is the pre-leukaemic middle ground.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What is the key blast cut-off separating MDS from AML?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: <20% blasts = MDS; ≥20% blasts = AML.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: How does MDS contrast with MPD (cross-reference)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: MPD = over-production of mature cells; MDS = ineffective production with dysplasia — same myeloid origin, opposite output.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What are the risk factors for MDS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Elderly — median onset >70 years, mostly primary/idiopathic; therapy-related — prior chemotherapy (alkylating agents) or radiotherapy (key secondary cause); benzene exposure (environmental).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What is the key secondary (therapy-related) cause of MDS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Prior chemotherapy (alkylating agents) or radiotherapy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: How does MDS typically present?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Often incidental — asymptomatic abnormal FBC. Symptoms arise from pancytopenia across three lines.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What are the clinical features of MDS by cytopenia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Anaemia → fatigue, pallor, shortness of breath; neutropenia → recurrent/severe infections; thrombocytopenia → purpura, bleeding.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What does the FBC and blood film show in MDS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Pancytopenia; often macrocytic anaemia (raised MCV — the classic film clue); blood film: dysplastic cells, blasts <20%; Pelger-Huët cells (bilobed neutrophils) and hypogranular neutrophils — named dysplasia findings, examinable.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What is the classic film clue for the anaemia in MDS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Macrocytic anaemia (raised MCV).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What are the named, examinable dysplasia findings on the MDS blood film?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Pelger-Huët cells (bilobed neutrophils) and hypogranular neutrophils.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What is the definitive investigation in MDS, and what does it confirm?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Bone marrow aspirate + biopsy = confirms hypercellular marrow, dysplastic lines, and blast %.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What drives prognosis in MDS, and give an example?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Cytogenetics drive prognosis — e.g. 5q- syndrome → lenalidomide-responsive.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What score guides treatment intensity in MDS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: IPSS score (International Prognostic Scoring System).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: How is low-risk MDS managed (supportive)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Watchful waiting; transfusions (RBC for anaemia); EPO (for anaemia in selected patients); infection management; iron chelation (transfusion overload — cross-ref haemochromatosis/thalassaemia).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: Why is iron chelation used in MDS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: For transfusion overload (cross-ref haemochromatosis/thalassaemia).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What is the targeted treatment for the 5q- subtype of MDS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Lenalidomide (a thalidomide analogue — the targeted exam fact).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: How is high-risk MDS (or younger/fit patients) managed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Hypomethylating agents (azacitidine), intensive chemo; allogeneic stem cell transplant = only cure (reserved for younger/fit patients given the elderly demographic).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What is the only cure for MDS, and why is it limited?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Allogeneic stem cell transplant — reserved for younger/fit patients given the elderly demographic.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: MDS discriminator — marrow cellularity in aplastic anaemia vs MDS vs AML?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Aplastic anaemia: hypocellular. MDS: hypercellular. AML: hypercellular.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: MDS discriminator — blood picture in aplastic anaemia vs MDS vs AML?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Aplastic anaemia: pancytopenia. MDS: pancytopenia. AML: blasts dominate.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: MDS discriminator — blast % in aplastic anaemia vs MDS vs AML?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Aplastic anaemia: not increased. MDS: <20%. AML: ≥20%.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: MDS discriminator — dysplasia in aplastic anaemia vs MDS vs AML?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Aplastic anaemia: no. MDS: yes. AML: not specified (—).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: MDS discriminator — trajectory of MDS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: MDS → AML.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: EXAM PEARL: State the MDS paradox.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Hypercellular marrow + peripheral pancytopenia = MDS (premature intramedullary apoptosis).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the single defining blast cut-off?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: <20% blasts = MDS; ≥20% = AML — the single defining cut-off.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: EXAM PEARL: In which demographic/context is MDS classic?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: MDS is pre-leukaemic — classic in the elderly or post-chemo/radiotherapy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: EXAM PEARL: What are the dysplasia clues on the film?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Macrocytic anaemia; Pelger-Huët / hypogranular neutrophils = dysplasia clues on film.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: EXAM PEARL: What targeted treatment matches the 5q- syndrome?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: 5q- syndrome → lenalidomide.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: EXAM PEARL: How does MDS differ from aplastic anaemia (the clean discriminator)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: vs aplastic anaemia: same pancytopenia but hypocellular marrow, no dysplasia — that is the clean discriminator.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What is the significance of the 5q- syndrome subtype of MDS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Del(5q) — good prognosis, macrocytic anaemia with a preserved or raised platelet count, older women, lenalidomide-responsive. Hallmark: hypolobulated ('non-lobulated') megakaryocytes on biopsy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What are the WHO MDS subtypes based on blast percentage?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: MDS with single lineage dysplasia (MDS-SLD); MDS with multilineage dysplasia (MDS-MLD); MDS with excess blasts 1 (5–9%); MDS with excess blasts 2 (10–19%); MDS with RS; 5q-.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What are the haematological features suggesting MDS transformation to AML?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Rising blast count approaching 20%, worsening pancytopenia, acquisition of new cytogenetic abnormalities, increasing transfusion requirements.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What does ring sideroblasts in MDS indicate and what gene is mutated?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Ring sideroblasts (iron-laden mitochondria around nucleus) indicate MDS-RS subtype. SF3B1 mutation drives this — associated with better prognosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: How does azacitidine work in MDS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Hypomethylating agent — incorporates into DNA, inhibits DNA methyltransferase → re-expresses silenced tumour suppressor genes → promotes differentiation and apoptosis of dysplastic clones.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What is the role of erythropoiesis-stimulating agents (ESAs) in MDS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: EPO or darbepoetin used in low-risk MDS with anaemia AND low serum EPO (<200 IU/L) — reduces transfusion requirements in ~40–50% of patients.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What is the IPSS-R (revised IPSS) and why is it used over the original IPSS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Revised IPSS — incorporates 5 cytogenetic risk groups, more granular Hb/platelet/neutrophil thresholds. Better stratifies into very low/low/intermediate/high/very high risk for treatment decisions.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: When is allogeneic SCT considered in MDS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Higher-risk MDS (IPSS-R intermediate/high/very high) in patients aged <65 with a suitable donor and adequate performance status. Only curative option.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: EXAM PEARL: What three things distinguish MDS from aplastic anaemia definitively?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: MDS: hypercellular (dysplastic) marrow, dysplasia in ≥1 lineage, and clonal cytogenetic abnormalities (blasts <20%; low-grade subtypes have <5%). AA: hypocellular marrow, no dysplasia, no excess blasts, normal cytogenetics.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.front: What are ring sideroblasts, and how do they relate to MDS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.back: Erythroblasts with iron-laden mitochondria forming a ring around the nucleus (seen on Prussian-blue stain). They define the MDS with ring sideroblasts (MDS-RS) subtype, often SF3B1-mutated, whose transfusion-dependent anaemia may respond to luspatercept.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: Von Willebrand disease: how common is it, inheritance, defect, and bleeding type?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Commonest inherited bleeding disorder; mostly autosomal dominant; deficiency/dysfunction of VWF; bleeding type is mucocutaneous.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: Haemophilia A & B: inheritance, factor deficiencies, and bleeding type?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: X-linked recessive — almost exclusively males. A = factor VIII deficiency; B = factor IX (Christmas disease). Bleeding type is deep (haemarthroses, muscle).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: What are the two jobs of VWF, and why does this explain haemophilia-like features in severe VWD?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: VWF has two jobs: (1) platelet adhesion/aggregation at the vessel wall; (2) carrier and stabiliser of factor VIII. That dual role explains why severe VWD can produce haemophilia-like features (low VIII, raised APTT).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: What is the core pathophysiology of von Willebrand disease?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: VWF deficiency → defective platelet function + secondary factor VIII deficiency.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: VWD Type 1: defect and key notes?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Partial reduction in VWF quantity. ~80% of cases; mildest; autosomal dominant.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: VWD Type 2: defect and key notes?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Qualitative / abnormal VWF. Autosomal dominant; subtypes (2A, 2B, 2M, 2N).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: VWD Type 3: defect and key notes?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Total absence of VWF. Autosomal recessive; severe — mimics haemophilia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: What are the mucocutaneous clinical features of VWD?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Gum bleeding on brushing, epistaxis; menorrhagia (often the presenting complaint); prolonged bleeding after dental/surgical procedures; easy bruising; positive family history (AD).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: What is often the presenting complaint of VWD?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Menorrhagia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: What are the investigation findings in VWD?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Raised bleeding time (PFA-100); APTT normal or raised (raised if VIII secondarily low); PT and platelets normal; low VWF antigen + activity; moderately low factor VIII; defective ristocetin-induced platelet aggregation — the specific diagnostic test.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: What is the specific diagnostic test for VWD?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Defective ristocetin-induced platelet aggregation.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: How is acute bleeding / pre-procedure VWD managed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Desmopressin (DDAVP) — releases endogenous VWF; first-line for type 1. VWF concentrate (± factor VIII) — for type 2/3 or severe bleeds. Tranexamic acid — antifibrinolytic for minor/mucosal bleeding.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: What is the menorrhagia ladder in VWD?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: 1. Tranexamic acid / mefenamic acid. 2. Norethisterone / COCP. 3. Mirena IUS. 4. Hysterectomy (last resort).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: Haemophilia A: factor deficiency, inheritance/carrier pattern, frequency, and desmopressin use?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Factor VIII deficiency; X-linked recessive (males affected, females carriers); the most common of the two; desmopressin useful in mild disease.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: Haemophilia B: factor deficiency, alternative name, comparison to A, and desmopressin use?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Factor IX deficiency; X-linked recessive; clinically identical to A. 'Christmas disease' — named after Stephen Christmas, the first patient described. Desmopressin is not effective.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: Why is haemophilia B called 'Christmas disease'?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: It is named after Stephen Christmas, the first patient described.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: Haemophilia severity grading: severe — factor level and bleeding pattern?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Severe: factor level <1% — spontaneous bleeds (haemarthroses, muscle haematomas from infancy).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: Haemophilia severity grading: moderate — factor level and bleeding pattern?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Moderate: factor level 1–5% — bleeds with minor trauma.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: Haemophilia severity grading: mild — factor level and bleeding pattern?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Mild: factor level 5–40% — bleeds only with significant trauma or surgery.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: What are the deep-bleeding clinical features of haemophilia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Haemarthroses — the hallmark (knees, ankles, elbows); muscle haematomas; prolonged post-surgical/traumatic bleeding; haematuria, GI bleeding; retroperitoneal haematoma; intracranial haemorrhage (severe disease).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: What is the hallmark clinical feature of haemophilia, and which joints?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Haemarthroses — knees, ankles, elbows.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: What are the investigation findings in haemophilia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Raised APTT; PT, TT, bleeding time, platelets, VWF — all normal; low factor VIII (A) or low factor IX (B) confirms diagnosis; Bethesda assay detects inhibitor antibodies.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: What does the Bethesda assay detect in haemophilia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Inhibitor antibodies.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: How is haemophilia managed with factor replacement?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: IV factor VIII or IX concentrate — on demand or prophylaxis. Severe disease: prophylaxis 3×/week from early childhood to protect joints. Desmopressin — mild haemophilia A only (releases stored VIII); ineffective in B. Tranexamic acid — adjunct for mucosal bleeding.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: In severe haemophilia, how is prophylaxis given and why?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Prophylaxis 3×/week from early childhood to protect joints.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: What are the complications and modern therapy considerations in haemophilia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Inhibitor antibodies — develop against infused factor, so treatment fails. Emicizumab (Hemlibra) — a bispecific antibody mimicking factor VIII; standard prophylaxis in haemophilia A including inhibitor patients. Chronic arthropathy from repeated haemarthroses. Historically HIV/HCV from plasma-derived products.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: What is emicizumab (Hemlibra) and its role?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: A bispecific antibody mimicking factor VIII; now standard prophylaxis in haemophilia A, including inhibitor patients.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: Discriminator table — inheritance of VWD vs Haemophilia A/B vs DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: VWD: autosomal dominant (mostly). Haemophilia A/B: X-linked recessive. DIC: acquired.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: Discriminator table — bleeding type of VWD vs Haemophilia A/B vs DIC?
