conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: VWD: mucocutaneous. Haemophilia A/B: deep (joints/muscle). DIC: mixed.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: Discriminator table — bleeding time in VWD vs Haemophilia A/B vs DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: VWD: raised. Haemophilia A/B: normal. DIC: raised.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: Discriminator table — APTT in VWD vs Haemophilia A/B vs DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: VWD: normal or raised. Haemophilia A/B: markedly raised. DIC: markedly raised.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: Discriminator table — PT in VWD vs Haemophilia A/B vs DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: VWD: normal. Haemophilia A/B: normal. DIC: raised.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: Discriminator table — platelets in VWD vs Haemophilia A/B vs DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: VWD: normal. Haemophilia A/B: normal. DIC: low.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: Discriminator table — factor VIII in VWD vs Haemophilia A/B vs DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: VWD: moderately low. Haemophilia A/B: markedly low (A only). DIC: low.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: Discriminator table — VWF / ristocetin in VWD vs Haemophilia A/B vs DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: VWD: abnormal. Haemophilia A/B: normal. DIC: not applicable.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: EXAM PEARL: How does the bleeding pattern tell you the level of the defect?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Mucocutaneous → VWF/platelet problem; haemarthrosis → coagulation factor (haemophilia).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: EXAM PEARL: What does an isolated raised APTT with everything else normal suggest?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Think haemophilia (or mild VWD). PT normal = intrinsic pathway only.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: EXAM PEARL: In which conditions does desmopressin work, and where does it NOT work?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Desmopressin works in haemophilia A (mild) and VWD type 1. It does NOT work in haemophilia B — there is no stored IX to release.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the one fact explaining the VWD/haemophilia overlap?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: VWF carries factor VIII — type 3 VWD → very low VIII → mimics haemophilia A.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the inheritance/carrier pattern of haemophilia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: X-linked recessive → haemophilia in males, carrier mothers. Daughters of affected males are obligate carriers.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.front: What is the role of gene therapy in haemophilia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.back: Single-dose AAV-vector gene therapies deliver the clotting-factor gene: valoctocogene roxaparvovec (haemophilia A) and etranacogene dezaparvovec (haemophilia B) are now approved — potentially transformative, reducing or removing the need for factor prophylaxis. Emicizumab (a factor VIII-mimicking bispecific antibody) remains standard prophylaxis in haemophilia A.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What is the decisive fork (consumption) in DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Massive coagulation activation consumes platelets and clotting factors faster than they are replaced — giving the paradox of clotting and bleeding simultaneously.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: Trace the consumption chain that produces the DIC lab picture.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Factors used up → PT/APTT/TT prolong; fibrinogen consumed → low; platelets consumed → thrombocytopenia; clots sheared in vessels → schistocytes; secondary fibrinolysis → raised FDPs/D-dimer.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: Is DIC ever a primary condition?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: No — DIC is always secondary; there is no primary DIC.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What is DIC (definition)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Widespread intravascular fibrin generation from massive coagulation cascade activation.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What is the core paradox of DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Too much clotting and too little clotting simultaneously — microvascular thrombosis plus haemorrhage.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What is the mechanism chain of DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Trigger → tissue factor exposed → coagulation cascade fires → fibrin + platelet consumption → secondary fibrinolysis → FDPs (which themselves worsen bleeding by inhibiting fibrin polymerisation) → haemorrhage + microvascular thrombosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: How do FDPs worsen bleeding in DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: They inhibit fibrin polymerisation.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What is the unifying mechanism behind all DIC triggers?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Anything that exposes or expresses tissue factor — endothelial damage, monocyte TF expression driven by cytokines, or direct TF release.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What is the commonest cause of DIC, and its mechanism?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Sepsis (especially Gram-negative) — cytokine-driven TF expression on monocytes.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: Which trauma/tissue destruction causes trigger DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Burns, major surgery, crush injury, fat embolism.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: Which obstetric causes trigger DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Amniotic fluid embolism, HELLP syndrome, placental abruption, retained products of conception.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: Which malignancy causes trigger DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Advanced solid tumours; APML (acute promyelocytic leukaemia) — the classic haematological trigger.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: Which transfusion and vascular causes trigger DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Transfusion reaction: ABO-incompatible transfusion. Vascular: aortic aneurysm, haemangioma.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What is the APML link to DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Acute promyelocytic leukaemia is the classic leukaemia trigger for DIC — promyelocytes release procoagulant granules. Treatment of APML (ATRA) itself initially worsens DIC.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What are the bleeding (haemorrhagic end) clinical features of DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Oozing from ≥3 unrelated sites (exam buzzword); venepuncture/cannula sites, IV lines; nose, mouth, gums; GI bleeding, haematuria; wound/surgical site bleeding.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What is the exam buzzword for the bleeding end of DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Oozing from ≥3 unrelated sites.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What are the thrombosis (thrombotic end) clinical features of DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Microvascular occlusion → end-organ ischaemia; AKI (renal cortical necrosis); delirium / reduced GCS (cerebral ischaemia); purpura fulminans (digital/skin necrosis); respiratory failure (ARDS pattern).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What is purpura fulminans in DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Digital/skin necrosis — a thrombotic feature.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What is the range of severity in DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: From subclinical (lab abnormalities only) to complete haemostatic failure.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: Investigations — what happens to platelets and PT/APTT/TT in DIC, and why?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Platelets very low (consumed in microthrombi); PT/APTT/TT all prolonged (clotting factors consumed).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: Investigations — what happens to fibrinogen and D-dimer/FDPs in DIC, and why?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Fibrinogen low (consumed — acute phase reactant, so may be normal early); D-dimer/FDPs markedly raised (secondary fibrinolysis).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: Investigations — what does the blood film and FBC show in DIC, and why?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Blood film: schistocytes (fragmented RBCs — sheared through fibrin strands in vessels). FBC: low Hb, low platelets (haemolysis + consumption).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: Why may fibrinogen be normal early in DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: It is an acute phase reactant, so it may be normal early despite being consumed.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: Discriminator — PT/APTT and fibrinogen in DIC vs liver disease vs TTP/HUS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: PT/APTT: DIC raised, liver disease raised, TTP/HUS normal. Fibrinogen: DIC low, liver disease low (late), TTP/HUS normal.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: Discriminator — D-dimer and schistocytes in DIC vs liver disease vs TTP/HUS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: D-dimer: DIC markedly raised, liver disease mildly raised, TTP/HUS normal/mildly raised. Schistocytes: DIC yes, liver disease no, TTP/HUS yes.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What is the key discriminator (Factor VIII) between DIC and liver disease?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Factor VIII is extrahepatic — normal/high in liver disease, but low in DIC. This is the key discriminator (TTP/HUS: Factor VIII normal).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What is Priority 1 in managing DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Treat the underlying cause — this is the only thing that reverses DIC. Antibiotics for sepsis, deliver in obstetric cases, treat APML. Everything else is supportive.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What supportive blood products are given in DIC, and when?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Only if bleeding or pre-procedure: platelets → keep >50 ×10⁹/L if bleeding; FFP → replaces all clotting factors; cryoprecipitate → replaces fibrinogen (target >1.5 g/L); red cells → for anaemia/blood loss. Treat the patient, not the numbers alone.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What does cryoprecipitate replace in DIC, and the target?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Fibrinogen — target >1.5 g/L.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What is the heparin exam trap in DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Heparin is considered only in thrombosis-predominant DIC (e.g. purpura fulminans, dominant microvascular clotting with minimal bleeding). Generally avoided when bleeding dominates. Frequently examined as a distractor — do not reach for heparin reflexively.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the DIC pentad?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Low platelets, raised PT/APTT, low fibrinogen, raised D-dimer, schistocytes. All five together = DIC until proven otherwise.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: EXAM PEARL: Why does 'DIC is always secondary' matter for management?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Because the most important management step is identifying and treating the underlying cause.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: EXAM PEARL: Summarise the triggers (sepsis, APML, obstetric).
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Sepsis = commonest trigger. APML = classic leukaemia link. Obstetric causes (amniotic fluid embolism, HELLP, abruption) are also high-yield.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: EXAM PEARL: When do you replace products in DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Treat the patient, not the numbers — only replace products (platelets, FFP, cryo) if actively bleeding or pre-procedure.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: EXAM PEARL: How does DIC differ from liver disease and TTP/HUS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: vs liver disease: factor VIII is extrahepatic — normal/high in liver disease, low in DIC. vs TTP/HUS: thrombocytopenia + schistocytes but normal coagulation screen.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: EXAM PEARL: Summarise the heparin trap in DIC.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Only consider in thrombosis-predominant DIC (purpura fulminans). Avoid when bleeding dominates — a common wrong-answer distractor.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What is the laboratory hallmark of DIC — the key 4-test combination?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: ↑PT, ↑APTT, ↓fibrinogen, ↑D-dimer/FDPs — simultaneous coagulation activation AND consumption. Thrombocytopenia present.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What is the underlying mechanism of DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Systemic thrombin activation → widespread microvascular clotting → consumption of clotting factors and platelets → secondary haemolysis and bleeding.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: What is the paradox of DIC clinically?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Simultaneous thrombosis AND bleeding — patients clot in microvessels (organ failure) but bleed from consumption of factors/platelets.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.front: EXAM PEARL: What differentiates DIC from liver failure on clotting tests?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.back: Both have ↑PT, ↑APTT, ↓fibrinogen — but DIC has markedly elevated D-dimer and schistocytes (MAHA), whereas liver failure has normal D-dimer and no fragmented cells.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What is the guiding principle of transfusion strategy?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: A restrictive transfusion strategy (lower thresholds) → better outcomes. Give one unit at a time, then reassess.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What is the indication for red cell transfusion?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: Anaemia / acute blood loss.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What are the red cell transfusion thresholds and targets in non-ACS vs ACS patients?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: Non-ACS: transfuse if Hb <70, target 70–90 g/L. ACS: transfuse if Hb <80, target 80–100 g/L.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What are the key practical facts for red cell transfusion (infusion time, storage, use-by)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: Infuse over 90–120 min; stored at 4°C; use within 4h.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: Which blood group is the universal donor for red cells?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: O negative.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What is the indication for FFP?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: Clotting factor deficiency (PT/APTT >1.5× normal).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What does FFP contain, who is the universal donor, and what is the caution?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: Contains all clotting factors. Universal donor = AB (no anti-A or anti-B). Large volume — avoid in fluid overload.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What is the indication for cryoprecipitate?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: Low fibrinogen (<1.5 g/L) — DIC, liver failure, massive transfusion.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What does cryoprecipitate contain, and where does the name 'cryo' come from?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: Concentrated fibrinogen, factor VIII, vWF, factor XIII. It is the precipitate of FFP at 4°C — hence 'cryo'.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What are the indications for platelet transfusion?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: Severe thrombocytopenia with bleeding; prophylactic if <10×10⁹/L.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: How are platelets stored, why, and what does one adult dose achieve?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: Stored at 20–24°C (NOT cold — cold causes aggregation). One adult dose raises the platelet count by ~20–30×10⁹/L.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What is the indication for PCC (prothrombin complex concentrate)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: Emergency warfarin reversal (major bleed, ICH, emergency surgery).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What does PCC contain, how fast does it work, and what must always be co-administered?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: Fastest reversal — within 1h. Contains factors II, VII, IX, X. Always give with IV vitamin K (factor VII has a short half-life → INR creeps back up).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What is the role of CMV-negative blood products and who are they used for?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: For immunocompromised patients and neonates. CMV is leucocyte-transmitted — leucodepletion makes most products effectively CMV-safe, but seronegative products are used for the highest-risk (transplant, HIV, pregnancy).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What do irradiated blood products do, and what do they prevent?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: T-cells in donor blood are depleted by irradiation. Prevents TA-GVHD (Transfusion-Associated Graft-versus-Host Disease) — fatal in immunocompromised patients (haematology, stem cell transplant).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: Summarise the transfusion thresholds for non-ACS vs ACS patients.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: Non-ACS: transfuse if Hb <70 → target 70–90 g/L. ACS: transfuse if Hb <80 → target 80–100 g/L.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: Why is a restrictive transfusion strategy preferred over a liberal one?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: A restrictive strategy (lower threshold) → fewer reactions, less fluid overload, and better outcomes than liberal.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What are the four steps of warfarin reversal?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: 1. Stop warfarin. 2. Vitamin K — IV (works in 4–6h) or oral (24h); always give. 3. PCC — for major bleed/ICH/emergency surgery, reversal within 1h, give WITH vitamin K. 4. FFP — older alternative; large volume, avoid in fluid overload.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: In warfarin reversal, how quickly does vitamin K work by IV vs oral route?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: IV works in 4–6h; oral works in 24h. Always give it.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: Why must vitamin K be given WITH PCC in warfarin reversal?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: Factor VII has a short half-life — without vitamin K, new factors won't be synthesised and the INR will rebound.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What is the universal first step for every transfusion reaction?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: STOP the transfusion.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: Febrile non-haemolytic transfusion reaction: cause, features, and management?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: Cause: anti-leucocyte antibodies → cytokine release. Features: fever, chills, rigors — mild, rise ≥1°C. Management: slow/stop; paracetamol; can restart if stable.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: Minor allergic transfusion reaction: cause, features, and management?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: Cause: reaction to donor plasma proteins. Features: urticaria, pruritus — no systemic compromise. Management: stop temporarily; antihistamine; can restart.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: Anaphylaxis during transfusion: cause, features, and management?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: Cause: IgA deficiency + anti-IgA antibodies. Features: hypotension, bronchospasm, angioedema — rapid onset. Management: STOP; IM adrenaline 0.5mg; ABC; IV fluids.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction: cause, features, and management?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: Cause: ABO incompatibility (wrong blood — human error). Features: fever, loin/back pain, hypotension, dark urine — onset within minutes. Management: STOP immediately; check patient ID + bag label; Coombs + recross-match; supportive.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: TRALI: cause, features, and management?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: Cause: donor antibodies → neutrophil activation → capillary leak. Features: non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema; hypoxia; HYPOtension; fever — within 6h. Management: STOP; O₂ + supportive; NO diuretics.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: TACO: cause, features, and management?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: Cause: volume overload (too fast / pre-existing HF/renal failure). Features: pulmonary oedema; HYPERtension; raised JVP; orthopnoea — cardiogenic. Management: slow/stop; furosemide + O₂; sit upright.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: TRALI vs TACO: what is the key discriminator?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: Both cause pulmonary oedema during/after transfusion — the key difference is blood pressure (and mechanism): TRALI = HYPOtension; TACO = HYPERtension.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: TRALI vs TACO: contrast mechanism and oedema type.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: TRALI: immune-mediated capillary leak, non-cardiogenic oedema. TACO: volume overload, cardiogenic oedema.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: TRALI vs TACO: contrast management.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: TRALI: O₂ + supportive, NO diuretics. TACO: furosemide + O₂.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: Give the one-line memory hooks for TRALI and TACO.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: TRALI — leaky lungs + low BP → no diuretics. TACO — too much fluid + high BP → diurese.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What is the maximum storage time and temperature for red cell concentrates?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: 35 days at 2–6°C.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What are the signs of an acute haemolytic transfusion reaction and its mechanism?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: Fever, rigors, loin pain, haemoglobinuria, hypotension — ABO incompatibility → complement activation → intravascular haemolysis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What is TACO and how does it differ from TRALI?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: TACO (Transfusion-Associated Circulatory Overload) — cardiogenic pulmonary oedema; responds to diuretics. TRALI (Transfusion-Related Acute Lung Injury) — non-cardiogenic; anti-leukocyte antibodies; PAOP normal; treat supportively.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What is the threshold for transfusing platelets prophylactically in a stable patient?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: <10 × 10⁹/L in stable patients; <50 × 10⁹/L pre-procedure; <100 × 10⁹/L for CNS/ophthalmic surgery.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What is irradiated blood and when is it used?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: Gamma-irradiated to destroy T-lymphocytes; used in immunocompromised patients (SCT, haematological malignancy, congenital immunodeficiency) to prevent transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease (TA-GvHD).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What is the indication for CMV-negative blood products?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: Since universal leucodepletion, standard UK components are 'CMV-safe.' CMV-seronegative products are now reserved for intrauterine transfusion, neonates (≤28 days), and elective (non-emergency) transfusion in pregnancy — no longer routinely for transplant recipients or HIV patients.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: What is the maximum dose of FFP and when is it given?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: 15 mL/kg; given for coagulopathy (PT/APTT >1.5× normal) especially in DIC, liver failure, or massive transfusion.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the transfusion trigger in a stable, asymptomatic patient without cardiac disease?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: Hb <70 g/L → transfuse; Hb 70–100 → clinical judgement; Hb >100 → generally avoid transfusion.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.front: EXAM PEARL: What are the four main delayed transfusion complications?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.back: Delayed haemolytic reaction (days–weeks); iron overload (repeat transfusions); alloimmunisation; transfusion-transmitted infection (rare).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What is the clinical significance and timing of neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: A medical emergency — the commonest serious complication of chemotherapy, typically 7–14 days post-cycle (the nadir).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What is the definition of neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Neutrophils <0.5 ×10⁹/L in a patient on anticancer treatment PLUS either temp >38°C or clinical signs of sepsis. (The diagnosis is a definition, not a judgement call.)

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: Why is neutropenic sepsis described as 'a definition, not a judgement call'?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: If the neutrophil and temperature/sepsis-sign criteria are met in a patient on anticancer treatment, the diagnosis is made — it is not a matter of clinical judgement.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: Why may the signs of neutropenic sepsis be blunted?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Without neutrophils there is less inflammatory response, so fever may be the only sign. The patient may be hypothermic, confused, or hypotensive instead — maintain a low threshold to treat.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What is the commonest organism in neutropenic sepsis, and where does it come from?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Staph epidermidis (coagulase-negative Gram-positive) — usually from indwelling lines in cancer patients.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: Why must empirical antibiotic cover in neutropenic sepsis target Gram-negatives including Pseudomonas?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Empirical cover must target Gram-negatives including Pseudomonas — this is why piperacillin-tazobactam (Tazocin) is chosen over narrow Gram-positive cover.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What is the key principle of the emergency response in neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Antibiotics are NOT delayed for investigations — give Tazocin first, take cultures around it.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: Emergency response Step 1: what is the first action and its timing?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: IV piperacillin-tazobactam (Tazocin) immediately — within 1 hour ('door-to-needle'), before cultures if needed.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: Emergency response Step 2: what cultures and septic screen are taken?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Cultures + septic screen: blood (peripheral and line), FBC, CRP, U&E, LFT, clotting, lactate; CXR, urine/sputum/stool.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: Emergency response Step 3: what is done if the patient is still febrile/unwell at 48h?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Escalate: meropenem ± vancomycin (vancomycin if line infection/MRSA suspected).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: Emergency response Step 4: what is done if the patient remains unresponsive at 4–6 days?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Investigate fungal infection → antifungals (e.g. amphotericin).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: When is vancomycin added in the escalation of neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: If line infection / MRSA is suspected (added to meropenem at the 48h escalation).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What is the de-escalation strategy in neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Switch to oral antibiotics once apyrexial for 48h; continue 10–14 days total.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What is the prophylaxis strategy for anticipated neutropenia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Anticipated neutrophils <0.5 → fluoroquinolone prophylaxis (e.g. ciprofloxacin) during the expected nadir; G-CSF (filgrastim) — shortens the duration of neutropenia in high-risk chemotherapy regimens.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What is the role of G-CSF (filgrastim) in neutropenic sepsis prophylaxis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: It shortens the duration of neutropenia in high-risk chemotherapy regimens.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: Which antibiotic is used for fluoroquinolone prophylaxis during the expected nadir?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Ciprofloxacin (a fluoroquinolone), when anticipated neutrophils <0.5.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: EXAM PEARL: State the neutropenic sepsis definition succinctly.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Neutrophils <0.5 + temp >38°C (or sepsis signs) on chemo = neutropenic sepsis — the definition is the diagnosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the rule about Tazocin timing?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Tazocin within 1 hour — do NOT wait for cultures or imaging.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: EXAM PEARL: Why may signs be blunted, and what should you beware?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: No neutrophils → muted inflammation; treat on a low threshold — beware hypothermia/confusion as the only signs.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the commonest organism vs what empirical cover targets?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Commonest organism: Staph epidermidis (lines), but empirical cover targets Pseudomonas/Gram-negatives.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the escalation ladder in neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Tazocin → meropenem ± vancomycin (48h) → antifungals (4–6 days).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the prophylaxis, and which notes cross-reference it?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Prophylaxis: fluoroquinolone ± G-CSF; cross-ref chemo complications (TLS, marrow failure).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What is the definition of neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Neutrophil count <0.5 × 10⁹/L (or <1.0 falling to <0.5) AND fever ≥38°C or clinical signs of sepsis. A haematological emergency — treat within 1 hour.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What is the most common source of infection in neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Gut translocation (gram-negative organisms — E. coli, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas) most common. Also: central line infections (gram-positive — Staph. aureus, Staph. epidermidis), lung, skin.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: Why is fever unreliable in neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Neutropenia ablates the inflammatory response — patients may be septic without high fever, or minimal localising signs. A temperature ≥38°C in neutropenia is always treated as sepsis regardless.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What initial investigations are performed in neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: FBC + differential (confirm neutropenia); blood cultures ×2 (peripheral + central line if present); CXR; urine MC&S; wound/exit site swabs; CRP, LFTs, U&E, lactate.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What is the first-line antibiotic in neutropenic sepsis per NICE?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Piperacillin/tazobactam (Tazocin) IV — broad-spectrum covering Gram-negatives including Pseudomonas. Meropenem if penicillin allergic or ESBL-risk.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: When is vancomycin added in neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Suspected line infection, Gram-positive bacteraemia, known MRSA, skin/soft tissue infection source, haemodynamic instability — add vancomycin for Gram-positive cover.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: When is antifungal therapy added in neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Persistent fever with prolonged neutropenia (>4–5 days) despite broad-spectrum antibiotics — add an empirical MOULD-active antifungal (liposomal amphotericin B or an echinocandin such as caspofungin); fluconazole is inadequate as it lacks Aspergillus cover. Consider CT chest for invasive fungal disease.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What is G-CSF (granulocyte colony-stimulating factor) in the context of neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: G-CSF (filgrastim) stimulates neutrophil production. Used prophylactically after high-risk chemotherapy to reduce neutropenic sepsis episodes. Occasionally used therapeutically in severe sepsis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What is the Multinational Association for Supportive Care in Cancer (MASCC) score?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Risk stratification tool for febrile neutropenia — identifies low-risk patients suitable for oral antibiotics/early discharge. Score ≥21 = low risk; <21 = high risk, admit for IV treatment.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: Which chemotherapy regimens carry the highest risk of neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Regimens with >20% febrile neutropenia risk (e.g. BEACOPP for HL, dose-dense AC for breast cancer, FLAG-IDA for AML) — G-CSF prophylaxis recommended.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What organisms cause early vs late neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Early (<7 days): Gram-negatives (E. coli, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas). Late (>7 days): Gram-positives (Staph., Strep.) and fungi (Candida, Aspergillus).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What is Hickman line-related bacteraemia and how is it managed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Coagulase-negative Staphylococci (Staph. epidermidis) colonise central lines. Treat with vancomycin ± line removal (required if tunnel infection, fungaemia, or failure to clear bacteraemia).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What prophylactic antibiotics are used in prolonged neutropenia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Fluoroquinolone prophylaxis (ciprofloxacin or levofloxacin) in patients expected to have neutropenia >7 days (e.g. induction chemotherapy for AML). Aciclovir for HSV/VZV reactivation prophylaxis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What antifungal prophylaxis is used in high-risk patients?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Fluconazole for Candida (haematology inpatients). Posaconazole for Aspergillus (AML induction, SCT — covers mould).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What are the signs of invasive pulmonary Aspergillosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Fever unresponsive to antibiotics, pleuritic chest pain, haemoptysis, nodular infiltrates on CT ('halo sign' = ground-glass halo around nodule). Treat with voriconazole IV.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: When should Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis (co-trimoxazole) be given?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: During prolonged immunosuppression: ALL treatment, high-dose steroids, alemtuzumab, SCT, AIDS-defining CD4 <200. Co-trimoxazole or dapsone (if sulfa-allergic).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: What is the 'sepsis six' in neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Oxygen; blood cultures (before antibiotics); IV antibiotics (within 1h); IV fluids; monitor urine output; lactate measurement. Applied within 1 hour of recognition — as per sepsis protocol but antibiotics are mandatory in neutropenia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the key time target in neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.back: Antibiotics must be given within 1 hour of presentation. Do not delay for investigations. Blood cultures before antibiotics ideally but do not delay antibiotics if cultures cannot be taken promptly.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: What is malaria, and how is it transmitted?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: A protozoan Plasmodium infection via the female Anopheles mosquito. The returning-traveller fever — suspect in anyone with fever who lives in or has travelled to an endemic area.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: What is the decisive fork in malaria (falciparum)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Falciparum — most severe, no dormant stage, RBC sequestration → complications (cerebral, AKI, DIC) → treat aggressively with IV artesunate.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: What is the decisive fork in malaria (vivax/ovale)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Vivax/ovale — milder but relapsing — hypnozoites in liver → need primaquine for terminal cure.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: What are the protective host factors in malaria (cross-ref sickle cell)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Sickle-cell trait, G6PD deficiency, thalassaemia, HLA-B53, Duffy-negative (specifically blocks vivax).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: Which protective host factor specifically blocks vivax?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Duffy-negative status.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: Life cycle: what happens after the mosquito injects sporozoites?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Mosquito injects sporozoites → liver (hepatocytes) → merozoites.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: Life cycle: what is unique to vivax/ovale in the liver stage?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Some hepatocytes form dormant hypnozoites → relapse weeks/months/years later.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: Life cycle: what happens once merozoites enter RBCs?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Hepatocyte ruptures → merozoites enter RBCs → replicate → rupture every 48h → haemolysis + pyrogen release → cyclical fever → more merozoites.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: Life cycle: what is the falciparum-specific RBC behaviour?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Infected RBCs adhere to small-vessel endothelium → sequestration/occlusion → cerebral malaria, AKI, etc.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: Species comparison — severity of falciparum vs vivax/ovale vs malariae?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Falciparum: most severe. Vivax/ovale: milder. Malariae: mild, chronic.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: Species comparison — liver dormancy in falciparum vs vivax/ovale vs malariae?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Falciparum: none. Vivax/ovale: hypnozoites → relapse. Malariae: none.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: Species comparison — fever pattern in falciparum vs vivax/ovale vs malariae?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Falciparum: irregular/continuous. Vivax/ovale: tertian (48h). Malariae: quartan (72h).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: Species comparison — incubation in falciparum vs vivax/ovale vs malariae?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Falciparum: 10–14 days. Vivax/ovale: 10–14 days. Malariae: 18 days–6 weeks.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: Species comparison — key risk in falciparum vs vivax/ovale vs malariae?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Falciparum: sequestration → complications. Vivax/ovale: relapse. Malariae: nephrotic syndrome (chronic).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: What are the symptoms and signs of malaria?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Symptoms: fever, rigors, profuse sweating, malaise, myalgia, headache, vomiting. Signs: pallor (anaemia), hepatosplenomegaly, jaundice (haemolysis → bilirubin).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: What are the falciparum complications (severe branch)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Cerebral malaria (seizures, coma); AKI — 'blackwater fever' (haemoglobinuria); pulmonary oedema/ARDS; DIC; severe haemolytic anaemia; hypoglycaemia; multi-organ failure.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: What is 'blackwater fever' in falciparum malaria?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: AKI with haemoglobinuria.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: Why is hypoglycaemia a classic trap in falciparum malaria?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: It is both a complication of the disease AND a quinine side-effect (a classic trap).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: What is the gold-standard investigation in malaria, and what do thick vs thin films show?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Blood films. Thick film — detects/screens for parasites (sensitivity). Thin film — identifies species + parasitaemia % (quantification).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: How many blood films are taken to exclude malaria, and why?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: 3 films over 3 days to exclude (48h cycle); high suspicion + negative → repeat at 12h and 24h.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: What additional investigations are used in malaria?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Rapid antigen tests (RDTs) — modern adjunct to film; parasitaemia >2% = suggests severe disease; FBC (anaemia, thrombocytopenia), LFTs, glucose, clotting (DIC screen).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: What parasitaemia level suggests severe disease?
How is uncomplicated malaria (oral) managed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Artemether-lumefantrine (Riamet) — first-line; atovaquone-proguanil (Malarone); quinine + doxycycline.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: What is the first-line oral treatment for uncomplicated malaria?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Artemether-lumefantrine (Riamet).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: How is severe/complicated malaria managed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: IV artesunate = treatment of choice (over IV quinine); admit all falciparum (risk of rapid deterioration). (Routine exchange transfusion for hyperparasitaemia is no longer recommended — withdrawn from UK/CDC guidance for lack of proven benefit.)

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: What is the treatment of choice in severe malaria, and when is exchange transfusion used?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: IV artesunate (over IV quinine) is the treatment of choice. Routine exchange transfusion for high parasitaemia is no longer recommended (withdrawn from 2016 UK and CDC guidance for lack of proven benefit).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: How is relapse prevented in vivax/ovale malaria?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Primaquine — clears hypnozoites from the liver (terminal prophylaxis). Check G6PD status first — primaquine causes haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: Why must G6PD status be checked before primaquine?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Primaquine causes haemolysis in G6PD deficiency.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: What is the malaria prophylaxis strategy?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Bite avoidance: nets, DEET, covering up; chemoprophylaxis per region: Malarone / doxycycline / mefloquine.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: EXAM PEARL: Why is falciparum 'the killer'?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: No relapse, but sequestration → cerebral malaria/AKI/DIC; admit all.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: EXAM PEARL: How is vivax/ovale relapse handled?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Relapse from hypnozoites → primaquine (check G6PD first — haemolysis risk).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the thick vs thin film rule and the exclusion sequence?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Thick film = detect; thin film = speciate + quantify; 3 negatives over 3 days to exclude.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: EXAM PEARL: What is first-line in severe malaria?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: IV artesunate = first-line in severe malaria (not IV quinine).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: EXAM PEARL: Summarise the fever patterns and malariae's chronic risk.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Tertian (48h) vivax/ovale; quartan (72h) malariae; malariae → nephrotic syndrome.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: EXAM PEARL: Summarise the protective factors and the exchange-transfusion threshold.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Protective: sickle trait, G6PD deficiency, thalassaemia, Duffy-negative (vivax) — cross-ref sickle cell. Note: routine exchange transfusion for high parasitaemia is no longer recommended (withdrawn from UK/CDC guidance); IV artesunate is the treatment for severe malaria.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: What is the WHO definition of severe malaria?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: P. falciparum malaria PLUS any one of: cerebral malaria (altered consciousness), severe anaemia (Hb <70), AKI, pulmonary oedema/ARDS, hypoglycaemia, circulatory collapse, or parasitaemia >5%.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: What is the treatment of falciparum malaria in pregnancy?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Quinine + clindamycin in 1st trimester (artemisinins avoided in 1st trimester). Artemisinins safe in 2nd/3rd trimester. Primaquine contraindicated in pregnancy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: What prophylaxis is recommended for travel to mefloquine-resistant areas (e.g. Thai-Cambodian border)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Doxycycline or Malarone (atovaquone-proguanil) — mefloquine resistance common in South-East Asian borders.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: Why is malaria in pregnancy particularly dangerous?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Placental sequestration of P. falciparum → low birth weight, maternal anaemia, hypoglycaemia, miscarriage, premature labour, maternal death. Pregnant women are 3× more susceptible.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the key 'returning traveller' clinical question?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: ANY fever in a returned traveller from an endemic area is malaria until proven otherwise. Take immediate blood films ×3 over 3 days. Do not wait for the classic fever pattern before testing.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: What is tafenoquine, and how does it compare with primaquine for vivax radical cure?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: A single-dose alternative to primaquine for radical cure of vivax malaria (clears liver hypnozoites). Like primaquine it causes haemolysis in G6PD deficiency, so quantitative G6PD testing is required first — and its long half-life makes that screening essential.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.front: What must be monitored after IV artesunate for severe malaria?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Malaria.back: Post-artesunate delayed haemolysis — check FBC weekly for ~4 weeks after treatment, as a delayed haemolytic anaemia is recognised even after successful parasite clearance.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: What is the decisive fork in thrombocytopenia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: Reduced production vs increased destruction. Is the marrow failing to make platelets, or are they made but consumed/destroyed?

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: What are the reduced-production (marrow fails) causes of thrombocytopenia, and the typical picture?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: Sepsis; B12/folate deficiency; liver failure (reduced thrombopoietin); leukaemia, MDS; drugs (valproate, methotrexate, isotretinoin, antihistamines, PPIs); alcohol. Usually comes with other cytopenias + abnormal marrow.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: What are the increased-destruction causes of thrombocytopenia, and the typical picture?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: ITP — immune (anti-GPIIb/IIIa); TTP — microangiopathic (ADAMTS13 low); HIT — immune (anti-PF4/heparin); HUS — microangiopathic (Shiga toxin); DIC — consumptive. Isolated low platelet count; normal/active marrow.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: What bleeding pattern does thrombocytopenia cause (cross-ref Haemophilia/VWD)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: Mucocutaneous / platelet-type bleeding — petechiae, purpura, epistaxis, gum bleeding, menorrhagia. (Deep joint/muscle bleeding = factor deficiency.)

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: Clinical features by count: what is the risk with a mild fall (100–150)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: Often asymptomatic / incidental.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: Clinical features by count: what is the risk with platelets <50?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: Easy bruising, prolonged bleeding, epistaxis, gum bleeding, menorrhagia, haematuria.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: Clinical features by count: what is the risk with platelets <10?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: High risk of spontaneous bleeding — ICH, GI bleed.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: ITP: what is the mechanism and demographics?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: Anti-GPIIb/IIIa antibodies (usually IgG) → platelet destruction. Children: acute, post-viral, self-limiting. Adults: chronic, women; can be 2° to SLE, CLL, HIV. Isolated thrombocytopenia — clotting normal.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: What investigations are used in ITP?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: Isolated thrombocytopenia; antiplatelet antibodies. Bone marrow (raised megakaryocytes) is not routine in typical ITP — reserve for atypical features or older adults (to exclude leukaemia/MDS before immunosuppression).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: When is a bone marrow indicated in ITP, and what does it show?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: Not routine in typical ITP — reserve for atypical features or older adults (to exclude leukaemia/MDS before immunosuppression). When done, it shows raised megakaryocytes.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: How is ITP managed (stepwise)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: 1. Oral prednisolone — 1st line. 2. IVIG — if urgent (pre-procedure/active bleed); raises count fast. 3. TPO-receptor agonists (eltrombopag/romiplostim) or rituximab — preferred 2nd line. 4. Splenectomy — now usually deferred (≥12 months) given infection/thrombosis risk.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: What is the first-line treatment for ITP, and what is used if urgent?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: Oral prednisolone is first-line; IVIG is used if urgent (pre-procedure/active bleed) as it raises the count fast.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: What is the mechanism of TTP?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: ADAMTS13 deficiency (inherited or autoimmune) → uncleaved vWF multimers → platelet microthrombi in small vessels → consumption (thrombocytopenia) + RBC shearing (MAHA).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: What are the causes of TTP?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: Idiopathic, post-infection; SLE, HIV, tumours; drugs (ciclosporin, OCP, clopidogrel, penicillin, aciclovir).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: What is the classic pentad of TTP?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: Fever, neurological signs, thrombocytopenia, MAHA (microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia), renal failure.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: How is TTP managed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: Plasma exchange — urgent, first-line (replaces ADAMTS13); steroids + rituximab; caplacizumab (anti-vWF nanobody, NICE-recommended add-on for acute acquired TTP); NEVER transfuse platelets unless life-threatening bleed — it fuels more thrombosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: Why must platelets not be transfused in TTP?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: It fuels more thrombosis (only transfuse in a life-threatening bleed).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: What is the mechanism of HIT (heparin-induced thrombocytopenia)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: Anti-PF4/heparin antibodies → platelet activation → paradoxical thrombosis AND thrombocytopenia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: What is the key clinical rule for HIT?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: Platelet fall typically 5–10 days after starting heparin; the timing is the diagnostic clue (4T score); it is paradoxical thrombosis, not just bleeding.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: How is HIT managed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: Stop heparin immediately; switch to an alternative anticoagulant (argatroban / fondaparinux / DOAC); NOT warfarin acutely; NOT platelet transfusion.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: In HIT, why avoid warfarin acutely and platelet transfusion?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: Warfarin is not used acutely and platelet transfusion is avoided; switch to an alternative anticoagulant (argatroban/fondaparinux/DOAC) instead.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: Discriminator table — mechanism of ITP vs TTP/HUS vs HIT vs DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: ITP: anti-GPIIb/IIIa. TTP/HUS: ADAMTS13 low / Shiga toxin. HIT: anti-PF4/heparin. DIC: consumptive.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: Discriminator table — clotting (PT/APTT) in ITP vs TTP/HUS vs HIT vs DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: ITP: normal. TTP/HUS: normal. HIT: normal. DIC: raised (deranged).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: Discriminator table — blood film in ITP vs TTP/HUS vs HIT vs DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: ITP: normal. TTP/HUS: schistocytes. HIT: normal. DIC: schistocytes.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: Discriminator table — clinical clue in ITP vs TTP/HUS vs HIT vs DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: ITP: isolated; post-viral child / adult woman. TTP/HUS: pentad (TTP) / renal+kids (HUS). HIT: thrombosis + heparin 5–10d. DIC: sick + bleeding + systemic cause.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: Discriminator table — key treatment in ITP vs TTP/HUS vs HIT vs DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: ITP: steroids / IVIG. TTP/HUS: plasma exchange. HIT: stop heparin. DIC: treat cause.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: EXAM PEARL: How does the production-vs-destruction fork narrow the diagnosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: The fork is reduced production vs increased destruction. Isolated thrombocytopenia + normal clotting → immune (ITP/HIT) or microangiopathic (TTP/HUS), not DIC.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: EXAM PEARL: Summarise ITP.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: ITP = isolated low platelets, anti-GPIIb/IIIa; prednisolone 1st line, IVIG for speed; bone marrow only if atypical features / older adult (not routine in typical ITP).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: EXAM PEARL: Summarise TTP.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: TTP = ADAMTS13 deficiency, pentad, plasma exchange; NEVER transfuse platelets — it worsens thrombosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: EXAM PEARL: Summarise HIT.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: HIT = paradoxical thrombosis, falls 5–10 days post-heparin; stop heparin, switch to alternative anticoagulant (not warfarin, not platelets).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the cleanest single discriminator on clotting?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: Clotting is normal in ITP/TTP/HIT; deranged in DIC — the cleanest single discriminator.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: EXAM PEARL: When are schistocytes present vs absent?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: Schistocytes = TTP/HUS/DIC (microangiopathy); absent in ITP/HIT.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: What is the platelet count threshold below which spontaneous bleeding occurs?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: <20 × 10⁹/L — spontaneous mucocutaneous bleeding (petechiae, purpura). <10 × 10⁹/L — spontaneous intracranial haemorrhage risk. >50 × 10⁹/L — safe for most surgical procedures.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: What is the mechanism of immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: Autoimmune — anti-platelet IgG antibodies (target GPIIb/IIIa or GPIb/IX) → splenic macrophage phagocytosis of opsonised platelets + reduced megakaryocyte platelet production.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: What is the treatment of severe acute ITP?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: First-line: prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day OR IV immunoglobulin (IVIg) 1 g/kg (faster response for bleeding). Second-line: rituximab, romiplostim (TPO receptor agonist), splenectomy (80% response, last resort).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: What is heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) and its paradox?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: HIT: anti-PF4/heparin antibody complex → platelet activation → paradoxical THROMBOSIS (not just bleeding) + thrombocytopenia (fall >50% or <100 × 10⁹/L). Stop all heparin; switch to argatroban or fondaparinux.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: What is thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) and its pentad?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: ADAMTS13 deficiency (acquired or inherited) → uncleaved vWF multimers → platelet microthrombi. Pentad: thrombocytopenia, MAHA (schistocytes), fever, neurological changes, renal impairment. Treat: plasma exchange + steroids.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: What is the 4T score for HIT?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: Thrombocytopenia (degree of fall), Timing (days after heparin start), Thrombosis (presence), oTher causes (excluded). Score 0–3 low probability, 4–5 moderate, 6–8 high. Act on moderate/high (stop heparin, anticoagulate).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: What is the mechanism of platelet destruction in drug-induced thrombocytopenia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: Drug acts as hapten binding to platelet surface protein → drug-dependent antibody → immune-mediated platelet destruction. Common drugs: quinine, vancomycin, abciximab, sulfonamides. Treat: stop offending drug.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.front: EXAM PEARL: What differentiates TTP from HUS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Thrombocytopeni.back: TTP: predominant neurological features, ADAMTS13 <10% (diagnostic). HUS: predominant renal features, often post-infectious (Shiga toxin from E. coli O157:H7), ADAMTS13 normal. Both: MAHA + thrombocytopenia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: What is the definition of pancytopenia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Reduction in all three cell lines — anaemia + neutropenia/leucopenia + thrombocytopenia. It is a pattern, not a disease — the task is always to find the cause.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: What is the decisive fork in pancytopenia, and what decides it?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Hypocellular marrow (production failure) vs cellular marrow (ineffective / destruction / infiltration) — decided by bone marrow biopsy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: What are the clinical features of pancytopenia, by cell line?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Anaemia → fatigue, pallor, SOB; neutropenia → infections (cross-ref Neutropenic Sepsis); thrombocytopenia → bruising, bleeding, petechiae (cross-ref Thrombocytopenia).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: Aetiology by marrow fork — primary marrow: what are the hypocellular vs cellular causes?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Hypocellular: aplastic anaemia. Cellular: MDS, acute leukaemia, myelofibrosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: Aetiology by marrow fork — infiltration: what are the hypocellular vs cellular causes?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Hypocellular: marrow replaced → empty of normal cells. Cellular: myeloma, lymphoma, metastatic carcinoma.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: Aetiology by marrow fork — what is the nutritional cause of pancytopenia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: B12/folate deficiency (megaloblastic — ineffective haematopoiesis); a cellular-marrow cause.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: Aetiology by marrow fork — which drugs/toxins cause pancytopenia (hypocellular)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Chemotherapy, radiation, chloramphenicol, carbimazole, methotrexate, alcohol.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: Aetiology by marrow fork — which infections cause pancytopenia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Viral (parvovirus, EBV, HIV, hepatitis), overwhelming sepsis (a hypocellular cause).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: Aetiology by marrow fork — what are the destruction/pooling causes of pancytopenia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Hypersplenism, PNH, SLE / autoimmune (cellular-marrow causes).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: Why is pancytopenia called the 'unifying presentation' across haematology?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: MDS, leukaemia, myelofibrosis, myeloma, lymphoma, and B12 deficiency are all structured notes — pancytopenia is the unifying presentation pointing at all of them.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: What is the definition of aplastic anaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Hypocellular ('empty') marrow replaced by fat — pancytopenia with no abnormal cells (no blasts, no dysplasia). This is the contrast with leukaemia/MDS.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: What are the causes of aplastic anaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Idiopathic/autoimmune (commonest); drugs; viral (EBV, hepatitis, parvovirus); radiation; inherited — Fanconi anaemia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: What is the commonest cause of aplastic anaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Idiopathic/autoimmune.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: What is the inherited cause of aplastic anaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Fanconi anaemia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: How is aplastic anaemia managed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Supportive: transfusions, infection control; immunosuppression: ciclosporin + ATG (+ eltrombopag — TPO-receptor agonist now in first-line triple therapy for severe aplastic anaemia); allogeneic stem cell transplant — curative in young patients.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: What is the curative treatment for aplastic anaemia in young patients?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Allogeneic stem cell transplant.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: What do FBC + reticulocytes show in the pancytopenia workup?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Confirm all three lines down. Low reticulocytes → production failure.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: Blood film clues: what do blasts vs dysplasia/Pelger-Huët cells indicate?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Blasts → leukaemia. Dysplasia / Pelger-Huët cells → MDS.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: Blood film clues: what do teardrop cells + leucoerythroblastic picture vs hypersegmented neutrophils + macrocytosis indicate?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Teardrop cells + leucoerythroblastic picture → myelofibrosis/infiltration. Hypersegmented neutrophils + macrocytosis → B12/folate deficiency.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: Blood film clue: what do schistocytes indicate?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Microangiopathy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: What is the role of haematinics (B12 and folate) in the pancytopenia workup?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: B12 and folate — always exclude the reversible nutritional cause first.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: What is the decisive test in pancytopenia, and what does it assess?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Bone marrow aspirate + trephine. Assesses cellularity (empty vs full); blasts, dysplasia, infiltration, fibrosis; dry tap → myelofibrosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: On bone marrow, what does a dry tap indicate?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Myelofibrosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: What supporting tests are used in the pancytopenia workup?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: LFTs; virology (HIV, hepatitis, EBV, parvovirus); autoantibodies (SLE); LDH (cell turnover marker); flow cytometry (CD55/CD59) for PNH — an aplastic-anaemia overlap.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: Discriminator table — aplastic anaemia: marrow cellularity, film clue, blasts, other?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Hypocellular; normal cells — just few; no blasts; no dysplasia, no splenomegaly.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: Discriminator table — MDS: marrow cellularity, film clue, blasts, other?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Hypercellular; dysplasia, Pelger-Huët; blasts <20%; macrocytosis; risk of → AML.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: Discriminator table — acute leukaemia: marrow cellularity, film clue, blasts, other?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Hypercellular; blasts; blasts ≥20%; Auer rods (AML).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: Discriminator table — myelofibrosis: marrow cellularity, film clue, blasts, other?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Fibrosed (dry tap); teardrop cells + leucoerythroblastic; blasts —; massive splenomegaly.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: Discriminator table — B12/folate deficiency: marrow cellularity, film clue, blasts, other?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Hypercellular; hypersegmented neutrophils, macro-ovalocytes; no blasts; raised LDH; low B12/folate; reversible.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: Discriminator table — hypersplenism: marrow cellularity, film clue, blasts, other?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Normal cellularity; normal film; no blasts; splenomegaly; peripheral pooling.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: EXAM PEARL: Why is pancytopenia never a final answer?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Pancytopenia is a pattern (all 3 lines down), never a final answer — always name the cause.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: EXAM PEARL: Summarise the marrow fork with examples.
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Hypocellular marrow → aplastic anaemia / drugs / radiation; cellular marrow → MDS, leukaemia, megaloblastic, infiltration.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the decisive investigation, and what are the best first clues?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Bone marrow biopsy is the decisive investigation; blood film + reticulocytes are the best first clues.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: EXAM PEARL: Which reversible cause must always be excluded first?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: B12/folate deficiency — cheap and fully reversible.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the three-way discriminator between aplastic anaemia, MDS, and leukaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Aplastic anaemia = empty marrow, no abnormal cells; MDS = full marrow + dysplasia; leukaemia = full marrow + ≥20% blasts.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: EXAM PEARL: What two emergencies sit inside pancytopenia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Neutropenic sepsis and severe bleeding (platelets <10) — cross-ref both notes.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: EXAM PEARL: What clinches a diagnosis of myelofibrosis within the pancytopenia workup?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Dry tap → myelofibrosis; teardrop cells + splenomegaly clinch it.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: What are the bone marrow findings that distinguish the four main causes of pancytopenia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Aplastic anaemia: hypocellular, fatty. MDS: hypercellular, dysplastic. Leukaemia/infiltration: hypercellular, blasts/abnormal cells. B12/folate deficiency: hypercellular, megaloblastic, no dysplasia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: What is haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) and how does it cause pancytopenia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: Uncontrolled macrophage activation → bone marrow macrophages phagocytose haematopoietic cells → pancytopenia + fever + splenomegaly + hyperferritinaemia (often >10,000 µg/L). Can be primary or secondary (infection, malignancy).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the 'pancytopenia screen' — the key investigations?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Pancytopenia.back: FBC + film (morphology); B12/folate; reticulocyte count; LFTs (liver failure, alcohol); TFTs (hypothyroidism); viral screen (EBV, CMV, HIV, parvovirus); bone marrow aspirate + trephine (definitive).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: What is the definition of polycythaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: Raised Hb / haematocrit / red cell count. It is a pattern, not a disease — the task is to classify the cause.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: What is the two-step decisive fork in polycythaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: 1. True (raised red cell mass) vs relative (low plasma volume). 2. If true → EPO low (primary/PV) vs EPO high (secondary).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: Why does polycythaemia matter clinically?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: Raised Hct → hyperviscosity → thrombosis (stroke, MI, DVT/PE) — the complication that makes it worth diagnosing and treating.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: Relative/apparent polycythaemia: what defines it, and what are the two subtypes with EPO levels?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: Normal red cell mass, low plasma volume. Dehydration — fluid loss concentrates RBCs (EPO normal); Gaisböck syndrome — middle-aged obese man, smoking, HTN, alcohol (EPO normal).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: True primary polycythaemia: what is the subtype, mechanism, and EPO?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: Polycythaemia vera (PV) — raised red cell mass; clonal marrow, JAK2 mutation (~95%); EPO LOW.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: True secondary polycythaemia: what are the appropriate (hypoxic) causes, and the EPO?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: Raised red cell mass, EPO-driven. Appropriate (hypoxic): chronic lung disease, high altitude, R→L cardiac shunt, heavy smoking (CO), OSA. EPO HIGH.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: True secondary polycythaemia: what are the inappropriate (tumour) causes, and the EPO?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: EPO-secreting tumours: renal cell carcinoma, hepatocellular, cerebellar haemangioblastoma, uterine fibroids. EPO HIGH.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: What is the single discriminating value in polycythaemia, and what does it separate?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: EPO is LOW in PV (autonomous marrow needs no stimulus) but HIGH in all secondary causes (something is driving it). This one result separates the dangerous clonal condition from everything reactive.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: Where does the full PV detail live (cross-reference)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: In the Myeloproliferative Disorders note; the Polycythaemia note carries a summary.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: What are the key features of polycythaemia vera?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: Clonal marrow, JAK2 V617F ~95%; low EPO; aquagenic pruritus (itch after hot bath); ruddy/plethoric complexion, conjunctival plethora; splenomegaly, HTN, gout; headache, visual disturbance, thrombosis; low ESR (hyperviscosity).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: What is aquagenic pruritus in polycythaemia vera?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: Itch after a hot bath.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: Why is the ESR low in polycythaemia vera?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: Hyperviscosity prevents sedimentation (low ESR).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: How is polycythaemia vera managed (stepwise)?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: 1. Venesection — 1st line; target Hct <0.45. 2. Aspirin — antiplatelet. 3. Hydroxycarbamide — cytoreduction for high-risk. 4. Ruxolitinib — JAK inhibitor for refractory.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: What is the first-line treatment for polycythaemia vera and its target?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: Venesection — first-line; target Hct <0.45.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: Secondary polycythaemia: what does 'appropriate (hypoxic)' mean and which causes fall under it?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: EPO correctly raised in response to hypoxia: chronic lung disease (COPD), high altitude, cyanotic heart disease (R→L shunt), OSA, heavy smoking (carboxyhaemoglobin).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: Secondary polycythaemia: what does 'inappropriate (tumour)' mean and which causes fall under it?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: EPO secreted autonomously: renal cell carcinoma (classic), hepatocellular carcinoma, cerebellar haemangioblastoma, uterine fibroids.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: What is the classic inappropriate (tumour) cause of secondary polycythaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: Renal cell carcinoma.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: How is secondary polycythaemia managed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: Treat the underlying cause (O₂/CPAP for hypoxia, resect tumour). Venesection only if symptomatic hyperviscosity.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: Investigations Step 1 — confirm and classify: what is done?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: Repeat FBC/Hct (exclude spurious); assess for dehydration (relative polycythaemia).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: Investigations Step 2 — what is the decisive test, and how is it interpreted?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: Serum EPO is the decisive test: low EPO → PV; high EPO → secondary.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: Investigations Step 3 — how is PV confirmed?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: JAK2 mutation testing — V617F positive in ~95% of PV; test JAK2 exon 12 if V617F-negative (covers most of the remainder).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: Investigations Step 4 — if secondary is suspected, what tests are done?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: ABG / SpO₂ — hypoxia; CXR / lung function — COPD; sleep study — OSA; abdominal imaging (CT/USS) — renal/hepatic tumour.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: What are the supporting findings in PV?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: Low ESR (high viscosity prevents sedimentation), raised urate (high cell turnover), splenomegaly on USS.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: EXAM PEARL: How do you approach polycythaemia as a pattern?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: Polycythaemia = a pattern (raised Hb/Hct) → classify: true vs relative, then EPO high vs low.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the single decisive discriminator on EPO?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: EPO low = PV (autonomous marrow); EPO high = secondary (hypoxia or tumour) — the single decisive discriminator.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: EXAM PEARL: What triad means PV until proven otherwise?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: JAK2 + low EPO + aquagenic pruritus = PV until proven otherwise.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: EXAM PEARL: How is relative polycythaemia characterised?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: Normal red cell mass, low plasma volume (dehydration, Gaisböck) — Hct raised but red cell mass is normal.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: EXAM PEARL: Summarise the secondary causes (appropriate vs inappropriate).
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: Appropriate (hypoxic — altitude, COPD, OSA, shunt) vs inappropriate (EPO-secreting tumour — renal cell carcinoma is classic).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: EXAM PEARL: What is the danger in true polycythaemia, and how is PV treated?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: Danger: hyperviscosity → thrombosis. Treat PV with venesection (target Hct <0.45) + aspirin.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: What is the haematocrit threshold that defines polycythaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: Haematocrit >0.52 in males, >0.48 in females (or Hb >185 g/L males, >165 g/L females). Red cell mass >125% of predicted confirms absolute polycythaemia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: What is apparent/relative polycythaemia and how does it differ from true polycythaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: Apparent (Gaisbock syndrome): normal red cell mass but reduced plasma volume (dehydration, diuretics, alcohol, obesity, smoking). True: increased red cell mass (primary = PV; secondary = ↑EPO).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.front: What are the causes of secondary polycythaemia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Polycythaemia.back: Appropriate (hypoxia-driven): COPD, sleep apnoea, altitude, cyanotic heart disease, high-affinity haemoglobin. Inappropriate (EPO-secreting tumours): renal cell carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, haemangioblastoma.
