conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: The single defining cut-off is <20% blasts = MDS and ≥20% = AML.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: A 72-year-old woman is found to have isolated del(5q) on cytogenetics, normal-to-high platelet count, and MDS on biopsy. What targeted treatment is available?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: 5q- syndrome responds specifically to lenalidomide (thalidomide analogue). It achieves cytogenetic remission in ~70% of 5q- MDS. Response is superior to other MDS subtypes.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: What is the role of azacitidine in MDS?
options: Hypomethylating agent used in higher-risk MDS to improve survival and delay AML transformation
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: Hypomethylating agent used in higher-risk MDS to improve survival and delay AML transformation
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: Azacitidine (hypomethylating agent) is standard treatment for higher-risk MDS (IPSS-R intermediate/high/very high). It improves OS and delays AML transformation compared to conventional care, but is not curative.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: Which MDS subtype is associated with SF3B1 mutation and has a better prognosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: SF3B1 mutation is found in >80% of MDS-RS cases (ring sideroblasts on Prussian blue stain). It is associated with better prognosis and predicts lenalidomide and luspatercept response.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: What is the significance of a rising blast count from 8% to 22% in a patient previously diagnosed with MDS?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: MDS transforms to AML in ~30% of cases. The threshold is ≥20% blasts (WHO criteria). Once transformation occurs, management shifts to AML protocols — intensive chemotherapy or palliation depending on fitness.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: A patient with MDS on regular transfusions develops cardiac and hepatic complications despite adequate haematological management. What is the likely cause?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: Repeated RBC transfusions deposit ~250 mg iron per unit. Iron accumulates in heart, liver, and endocrine organs. Cardiac complications (arrhythmia, cardiomyopathy) and hepatic cirrhosis result. Iron chelation (deferasirox oral or desferrioxamine SC/IV) is indicated.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: What EPO level predicts response to ESA therapy in MDS?
options: Serum EPO <200 IU/L — low endogenous EPO suggests ESA will be effective
EPO level is irrelevant to response
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: Serum EPO <200 IU/L — low endogenous EPO suggests ESA will be effective
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: ESAs (EPO/darbepoetin) work best in low-risk MDS with serum EPO <200 IU/L. High endogenous EPO suggests the marrow is already maximally stimulated and ESAs add little benefit.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: Why is allogeneic SCT limited in MDS despite being the only cure?
options: MDS is predominantly a disease of the elderly (median age >70) who cannot tolerate intensive conditioning
Donor availability is never an issue
MDS is always cured with azacitidine
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: MDS is predominantly a disease of the elderly (median age >70) who cannot tolerate intensive conditioning
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: Allogeneic SCT carries significant treatment-related morbidity/mortality (10–20%). Since MDS predominantly affects patients >70 years, most are ineligible. Reduced-intensity conditioning expands eligibility to older/fitter patients.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: What differentiates MDS from aplastic anaemia (AA) on bone marrow biopsy?
options: MDS: hypercellular with dysplasia; AA: hypocellular without dysplasia
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: MDS: hypercellular with dysplasia; AA: hypocellular without dysplasia
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: The key bone marrow distinction: MDS = hypercellular with dysplastic cell lines and ±increased blasts. AA = hypocellular (fatty marrow replacement) with no dysplasia. Both cause pancytopenia but via opposite marrow patterns.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: What does an Hb of 82 g/L with MCV 104 fL, platelet count 68, and neutrophil count 0.9 suggest in a 68-year-old man?
options: MDS with pancytopenia and macrocytic anaemia
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.answer: MDS with pancytopenia and macrocytic anaemia
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: Pancytopenia with macrocytic anaemia in an elderly patient without obvious nutritional deficiency (normal B12/folate) should prompt bone marrow aspirate to diagnose MDS. Macrocytosis is a classic MDS film finding.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.question: EXAM PEARL: A 74-year-old man post-chemotherapy for bladder cancer presents 3 years later with fatigue, pancytopenia, and hypercellular dysplastic marrow with 12% blasts. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Myelodysplasia.explanation: Therapy-related MDS (t-MDS) occurs 3–7 years after alkylating agent chemotherapy or radiotherapy. Blasts 10–19% = MDS with excess blasts 2 (MEB2). t-MDS carries worse prognosis than primary MDS.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: Which is the commonest inherited bleeding disorder, and what is its usual inheritance?
options: Von Willebrand disease — mostly autosomal dominant
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Von Willebrand disease — mostly autosomal dominant
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Von Willebrand disease is the commonest inherited bleeding disorder and is mostly autosomal dominant.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: Which factor is deficient in haemophilia A versus haemophilia B?
options: A = factor VIII; B = factor IX
A = factor IX; B = factor VIII
A = factor VII; B = factor IX
A = factor IX; B = factor XI
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: A = factor VIII; B = factor IX
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Haemophilia A is factor VIII deficiency; haemophilia B is factor IX deficiency (Christmas disease).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: What are the two jobs of VWF, and why does this explain haemophilia-like features in severe VWD?
options: Platelet adhesion/aggregation and carrier/stabiliser of factor VIII — so severe VWD lowers VIII and raises APTT
Carrier of factor IX and platelet inhibition
Complement activation and factor VIII degradation
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Platelet adhesion/aggregation and carrier/stabiliser of factor VIII — so severe VWD lowers VIII and raises APTT
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: VWF has two jobs: platelet adhesion/aggregation at the vessel wall, and carrier/stabiliser of factor VIII. That dual role explains why severe VWD can produce haemophilia-like features (low VIII, raised APTT).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: What is the core pathophysiology of von Willebrand disease?
options: VWF deficiency → defective platelet function + secondary factor VIII deficiency
Factor IX deficiency → impaired intrinsic pathway
Consumption of clotting factors and platelets
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: VWF deficiency → defective platelet function + secondary factor VIII deficiency
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: VWD is VWF deficiency → defective platelet function + secondary factor VIII deficiency.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: Which VWD type accounts for ~80% of cases, is mildest, and is autosomal dominant?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Type 1 (partial reduction in VWF quantity)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Type 1 is a partial reduction in VWF quantity, ~80% of cases, mildest, and autosomal dominant.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: Which VWD type is a total absence of VWF, autosomal recessive, and mimics haemophilia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Type 3
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Type 3 is a total absence of VWF, autosomal recessive, severe, and mimics haemophilia.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: A young woman presents with gum bleeding on brushing, epistaxis, easy bruising and heavy periods, with a positive family history. What is often the presenting complaint of VWD?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Menorrhagia
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Menorrhagia is often the presenting complaint of VWD, alongside mucocutaneous bleeding (gum bleeding, epistaxis, easy bruising) and a positive family history.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: What is the specific diagnostic test for von Willebrand disease?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Defective ristocetin-induced platelet aggregation
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Defective ristocetin-induced platelet aggregation is the specific diagnostic test for VWD.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: Which investigation pattern fits VWD?
options: Raised bleeding time; PT and platelets normal; low VWF antigen + activity; moderately low factor VIII
Normal bleeding time; low platelets; raised PT
Raised PT only with normal APTT
Low platelets with abnormal VWF and raised PT
Normal VWF with markedly low factor IX
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Raised bleeding time; PT and platelets normal; low VWF antigen + activity; moderately low factor VIII
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: VWD shows raised bleeding time (PFA-100), normal PT and platelets, low VWF antigen + activity, moderately low factor VIII, and defective ristocetin-induced platelet aggregation. APTT may be normal or raised.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: What is the first-line treatment for acute bleeding/pre-procedure in type 1 VWD?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Desmopressin (DDAVP) — releases endogenous VWF
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Desmopressin (DDAVP), which releases endogenous VWF, is first-line for type 1; VWF concentrate (± factor VIII) is for type 2/3 or severe bleeds; tranexamic acid for minor/mucosal bleeding.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: What is the first step of the menorrhagia ladder in VWD?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Tranexamic acid / mefenamic acid
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: The menorrhagia ladder is: 1) tranexamic acid / mefenamic acid, 2) norethisterone / COCP, 3) Mirena IUS, 4) hysterectomy (last resort).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: Which is the most common of the two haemophilias, and is desmopressin useful in it?
options: Haemophilia A — desmopressin useful in mild disease
Haemophilia B — desmopressin useful in mild disease
Both equally common — desmopressin equally effective
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Haemophilia A — desmopressin useful in mild disease
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Haemophilia A (factor VIII) is the most common of the two, and desmopressin is useful in mild disease.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: Why is haemophilia B called 'Christmas disease'?
options: Named after Stephen Christmas, the first patient described
Because it was discovered on Christmas Day
After the doctor who described it
Because of the festive rash it causes
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Named after Stephen Christmas, the first patient described
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Haemophilia B is 'Christmas disease', named after Stephen Christmas, the first patient described.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: A boy with haemophilia has spontaneous haemarthroses and muscle haematomas from infancy. What factor level defines this severe grade?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Severe haemophilia is a factor level <1%, with spontaneous bleeds — haemarthroses and muscle haematomas from infancy.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: A patient with haemophilia bleeds only with significant trauma or surgery. Which severity grade and factor level is this?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Mild — 5–40%
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Mild haemophilia has a factor level of 5–40% and bleeds only with significant trauma or surgery.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: What is the hallmark clinical feature of haemophilia, and which joints are typically affected?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Haemarthroses — knees, ankles, elbows
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Haemarthroses are the hallmark of haemophilia, typically affecting the knees, ankles, and elbows.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: Which investigation pattern fits haemophilia?
options: Raised APTT; PT, TT, bleeding time, platelets, VWF all normal; low factor VIII (A) or IX (B) confirms
Low platelets with raised bleeding time
Raised bleeding time with normal APTT
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Raised APTT; PT, TT, bleeding time, platelets, VWF all normal; low factor VIII (A) or IX (B) confirms
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Haemophilia shows a raised APTT with PT, TT, bleeding time, platelets, and VWF all normal; low factor VIII (A) or factor IX (B) confirms the diagnosis. The Bethesda assay detects inhibitor antibodies.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: What does the Bethesda assay detect in haemophilia?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Inhibitor antibodies
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: The Bethesda assay detects inhibitor antibodies.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: How is factor replacement given in severe haemophilia?
options: IV factor VIII or IX concentrate as prophylaxis 3×/week from early childhood to protect joints
Desmopressin for both A and B
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: IV factor VIII or IX concentrate as prophylaxis 3×/week from early childhood to protect joints
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Severe disease is managed with IV factor VIII or IX concentrate as prophylaxis 3×/week from early childhood to protect the joints.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: What is emicizumab (Hemlibra), and what is its role?
options: A bispecific antibody mimicking factor VIII; standard prophylaxis in haemophilia A including inhibitor patients
A factor IX concentrate for haemophilia B
A VWF concentrate for type 3 VWD
A monoclonal antibody targeting complement C5
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: A bispecific antibody mimicking factor VIII; standard prophylaxis in haemophilia A including inhibitor patients
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Emicizumab (Hemlibra) is a bispecific antibody mimicking factor VIII, now standard prophylaxis in haemophilia A, including inhibitor patients.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: Which complication of haemophilia therapy causes treatment to fail?
options: Inhibitor antibodies developing against infused factor
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Inhibitor antibodies developing against infused factor
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Inhibitor antibodies develop against infused factor, causing treatment to fail; chronic arthropathy from repeated haemarthroses and historically HIV/HCV from plasma-derived products are other complications.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: In the discriminator table, what is the inheritance of VWD vs Haemophilia A/B vs DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Autosomal dominant (mostly); X-linked recessive; acquired
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Inheritance: VWD is autosomal dominant (mostly), haemophilia A/B is X-linked recessive, and DIC is acquired.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: In the discriminator table, what is the bleeding type of VWD vs Haemophilia A/B vs DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Mucocutaneous; deep (joints/muscle); mixed
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Bleeding type: VWD is mucocutaneous, haemophilia A/B is deep (joints/muscle), and DIC is mixed.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: In the discriminator table, how do platelets compare across VWD, Haemophilia A/B, and DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Normal; normal; low
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Platelets are normal in VWD, normal in haemophilia A/B, and low in DIC.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: In the discriminator table, how does PT compare across VWD, Haemophilia A/B, and DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Normal; normal; raised
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: PT is normal in VWD, normal in haemophilia A/B, and raised in DIC.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: In the discriminator table, how does the VWF / ristocetin result compare across VWD, Haemophilia A/B, and DIC?
options: Abnormal in VWD; normal in Haemophilia A/B; not applicable in DIC
Normal in VWD; abnormal in Haemophilia A/B
Not applicable in VWD; abnormal in Haemophilia A/B
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Abnormal in VWD; normal in Haemophilia A/B; not applicable in DIC
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: VWF / ristocetin is abnormal in VWD, normal in haemophilia A/B, and not applicable in DIC.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: EXAM PEARL: A patient has mucocutaneous bleeding. What level of the haemostatic system does this point to, versus haemarthrosis?
options: Mucocutaneous → VWF/platelet problem; haemarthrosis → coagulation factor (haemophilia)
Mucocutaneous → coagulation factor; haemarthrosis → platelet problem
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Mucocutaneous → VWF/platelet problem; haemarthrosis → coagulation factor (haemophilia)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Bleeding pattern tells you the level: mucocutaneous → VWF/platelet problem; haemarthrosis → coagulation factor (haemophilia).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: EXAM PEARL: An isolated raised APTT with normal everything else (including PT) suggests what?
options: Haemophilia (or mild VWD) — intrinsic pathway only
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Haemophilia (or mild VWD) — intrinsic pathway only
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: An isolated raised APTT with normal everything else (and normal PT) points to haemophilia or mild VWD — the intrinsic pathway only.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: EXAM PEARL: In which conditions does desmopressin work, and where does it NOT work, and why?
options: Works in haemophilia A (mild) and VWD type 1; does NOT work in haemophilia B — no stored IX to release
Works in haemophilia B; does not work in haemophilia A
Works in all haemophilia and all VWD types
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Works in haemophilia A (mild) and VWD type 1; does NOT work in haemophilia B — no stored IX to release
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Desmopressin works in mild haemophilia A and VWD type 1, but does NOT work in haemophilia B because there is no stored factor IX to release.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: EXAM PEARL: What is the single fact explaining the VWD/haemophilia overlap, and which VWD type mimics haemophilia A?
options: VWF carries factor VIII; type 3 VWD → very low VIII → mimics haemophilia A
VWF carries factor IX; type 1 VWD → mimics haemophilia B
Factor VIII carries VWF; type 2 VWD → mimics haemophilia A
VWF degrades factor VIII; type 3 VWD → mimics DIC
VWF and factor VIII are unrelated
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: VWF carries factor VIII; type 3 VWD → very low VIII → mimics haemophilia A
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: VWF carries factor VIII — the one fact explaining the VWD/haemophilia overlap; type 3 VWD gives very low VIII and so mimics haemophilia A.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: A 7-year-old boy presents with spontaneous haemarthrosis and a prolonged APTT with normal PT. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Haemophilia A (factor VIII deficiency)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Haemophilia A presents with spontaneous haemarthroses, deep muscle bleeds, and prolonged APTT with normal PT. It is X-linked recessive (males affected). Haemophilia A (factor VIII) is 4× more common than haemophilia B (factor IX).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: What is the inheritance pattern of haemophilia A and B?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: X-linked recessive
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Both haemophilia A (factor VIII) and haemophilia B (factor IX) are X-linked recessive. Males are affected; females are carriers. Daughters of affected males are obligate carriers.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: Which clotting test is abnormal in haemophilia A?
options: PT prolonged; APTT normal; bleeding time prolonged
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: APTT prolonged; PT normal
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Factor VIII is in the intrinsic pathway (APTT measures). PT measures extrinsic pathway (factor VII, X, V, II) which is unaffected. Platelet function and bleeding time are normal.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: What is the treatment for acute haemarthrosis in a patient with severe haemophilia A?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Recombinant factor VIII concentrate
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Recombinant factor VIII concentrate is the treatment of choice for haemophilia A bleeds. Target factor VIII level >50% for joint bleeds, >80–100% for life-threatening bleeds. DDAVP can be used for mild haemophilia A only.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: How does DDAVP (desmopressin) help in mild haemophilia A?
options: Stimulates release of stored factor VIII and vWF from endothelial cells
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Stimulates release of stored factor VIII and vWF from endothelial cells
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: DDAVP causes endothelial cells to release stored factor VIII and vWF, temporarily raising levels 2–4 fold. Useful for minor bleeds or procedures in mild haemophilia A and type 1 vWD. Not effective in severe haemophilia A.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: What is the most common inherited bleeding disorder?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Von Willebrand disease
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: vWD affects ~1% of the population and is the most common inherited bleeding disorder. Most cases are type 1 (partial quantitative deficiency of vWF). It is autosomal dominant (unlike haemophilia which is X-linked).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: A young woman presents with menorrhagia, easy bruising, and prolonged bleeding after dental extraction. APTT and bleeding time are prolonged. What is the likely diagnosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Von Willebrand disease type 1
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: vWD classically presents with mucocutaneous bleeding (menorrhagia, gum bleeding, easy bruising, epistaxis, post-procedure bleeding). APTT may be prolonged (vWF stabilises factor VIII). Bleeding time prolonged due to platelet adhesion defect.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: What is type 3 von Willebrand disease?
options: Complete absence of vWF — most severe form, behaves like haemophilia A
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Complete absence of vWF — most severe form, behaves like haemophilia A
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Type 3 vWD is rare (autosomal recessive) with complete vWF absence. Secondary factor VIII deficiency occurs (vWF stabilises VIII), causing haemophilia A-like bleeds in addition to mucocutaneous bleeding.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: What is the prophylaxis strategy in severe haemophilia A?
options: Regular prophylactic factor VIII infusions 3× weekly
On-demand treatment only when bleeding occurs
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Regular prophylactic factor VIII infusions 3× weekly
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Prophylactic factor VIII (3× weekly or every other day) prevents haemarthroses and joint damage in severe haemophilia A. Newer extended half-life products (emicizumab, a bispecific antibody) allow less frequent dosing.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.question: EXAM PEARL: What differentiates haemophilia A from vWD on lab testing?
options: Haemophilia A: prolonged APTT, normal bleeding time; vWD: prolonged APTT AND prolonged bleeding time
Haemophilia A: both PT and APTT prolonged; vWD: PT only
Haemophilia A: normal APTT; vWD: prolonged PT
Haemophilia A: platelet count low; vWD: platelet count normal
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.answer: Haemophilia A: prolonged APTT, normal bleeding time; vWD: prolonged APTT AND prolonged bleeding time
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Haemophilia / V.explanation: Haemophilia A: APTT prolonged (factor VIII deficiency), normal platelet function (normal bleeding time). vWD: APTT prolonged (vWF stabilises factor VIII) AND bleeding time prolonged (vWF needed for platelet adhesion at vessel wall).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: What is the guiding principle of transfusion strategy?
options: Restrictive transfusion strategy (lower thresholds) → better outcomes; one unit at a time, then reassess
Always transfuse two units before reassessing
Transfuse to a target Hb of 120 g/L in all patients
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Restrictive transfusion strategy (lower thresholds) → better outcomes; one unit at a time, then reassess
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: A restrictive transfusion strategy (lower thresholds) leads to better outcomes; give one unit at a time, then reassess.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: A patient without ACS has symptomatic anaemia. At what Hb threshold should red cells be transfused, and to what target?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Transfuse if Hb <70, target 70–90 g/L
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: In non-ACS patients, transfuse if Hb <70 with a target of 70–90 g/L.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: A patient with acute coronary syndrome is anaemic. What is the red cell transfusion threshold and target?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Transfuse if Hb <80, target 80–100 g/L
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: In ACS, transfuse if Hb <80 with a target of 80–100 g/L.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: Which set of practical facts is correct for red cell transfusion?
options: Infuse over 90–120 min; stored at 4°C; use within 4h
Infuse over 30 min; stored at 20–24°C; use within 24h
Infuse over 4h; stored at room temperature; use within 1h
Infuse over 10 min; stored at -20°C; use within 6h
Infuse over 6h; stored at 4°C; use within 48h
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Infuse over 90–120 min; stored at 4°C; use within 4h
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Red cells are infused over 90–120 min, stored at 4°C, and used within 4h.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: Which blood group is the universal donor for red cells?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: O negative
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: O negative is the universal donor for red cells.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: What is the indication for FFP?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Clotting factor deficiency (PT/APTT >1.5× normal)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: FFP is indicated for clotting factor deficiency (PT/APTT >1.5× normal).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: Which statement about FFP is correct?
options: Contains all clotting factors; universal donor = AB; avoid in fluid overload (large volume)
Contains only fibrinogen; universal donor = O
Contains factors II, VII, IX, X only
Is the fastest option for warfarin reversal
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Contains all clotting factors; universal donor = AB; avoid in fluid overload (large volume)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: FFP contains all clotting factors, its universal donor is AB (no anti-A or anti-B), and it is a large volume so should be avoided in fluid overload.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: A patient with DIC has a fibrinogen of 1.0 g/L. Which product is indicated, and what does it contain?
options: Cryoprecipitate — fibrinogen, factor VIII, vWF, factor XIII
PCC — factors II, VII, IX, X
Red cells — for acute blood loss
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Cryoprecipitate — fibrinogen, factor VIII, vWF, factor XIII
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Cryoprecipitate is indicated for low fibrinogen (<1.5 g/L) — DIC, liver failure, massive transfusion — and contains fibrinogen, factor VIII, vWF, and factor XIII.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: Why is cryoprecipitate called 'cryo'?
options: It is the precipitate of FFP at 4°C
It is frozen at -80°C before use
It is stored on dry ice
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: It is the precipitate of FFP at 4°C
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Cryoprecipitate is the precipitate of FFP at 4°C — hence 'cryo'.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: What is the prophylactic platelet transfusion threshold?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Platelets are indicated for severe thrombocytopenia with bleeding, and prophylactically if <10×10⁹/L.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: How are platelets stored, and why are they not refrigerated?
options: Stored at 20–24°C because cold causes aggregation
Stored at 37°C to mimic body temperature
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Stored at 20–24°C because cold causes aggregation
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Platelets are stored at 20–24°C (NOT cold — cold causes aggregation).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: By how much does one adult dose of platelets typically raise the platelet count?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: One adult dose of platelets raises the platelet count by ~20–30×10⁹/L.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: A patient on warfarin presents with an intracranial haemorrhage. Which product gives the fastest reversal, and which factors does it contain?
options: PCC — factors II, VII, IX, X (reversal within 1h)
Platelets — factors II, VII, IX, X
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: PCC — factors II, VII, IX, X (reversal within 1h)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: PCC gives the fastest reversal (within 1h) for emergency warfarin reversal and contains factors II, VII, IX, X.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: Why must IV vitamin K always be given alongside PCC for warfarin reversal?
options: Factor VII has a short half-life, so without vitamin K the INR creeps back up
Vitamin K speeds up PCC infusion
Vitamin K prevents an allergic reaction to PCC
Vitamin K reverses the action of platelets
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Factor VII has a short half-life, so without vitamin K the INR creeps back up
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Always give PCC with IV vitamin K because factor VII has a short half-life — without it, new factors won't be synthesised and the INR will rebound.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: Which product is indicated for immunocompromised patients and neonates because CMV is leucocyte-transmitted?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: CMV-negative products
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: CMV-negative products are for immunocompromised patients and neonates; CMV is leucocyte-transmitted, and seronegative products are used for the highest-risk groups (transplant, HIV, pregnancy).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: What do irradiated blood products prevent, and how?
options: T-cells depleted by irradiation → prevents TA-GVHD
Plasma proteins removed → prevents allergic reactions
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: T-cells depleted by irradiation → prevents TA-GVHD
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Irradiation depletes donor T-cells, preventing TA-GVHD (Transfusion-Associated Graft-versus-Host Disease), which is fatal in immunocompromised patients (haematology, stem cell transplant).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: Why does a restrictive transfusion strategy give better outcomes than a liberal one?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Fewer reactions, less fluid overload
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: A restrictive strategy (lower threshold) results in fewer reactions, less fluid overload, and better outcomes than liberal.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: In warfarin reversal, how quickly does vitamin K work by the IV versus oral route?
options: IV works in 4–6h; oral works in 24h
IV works in 24h; oral works in 4–6h
IV works in 1h; oral works in 12h
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: IV works in 4–6h; oral works in 24h
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Vitamin K works in 4–6h by IV and in 24h orally; it should always be given.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: What is the universal first step for every transfusion reaction?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: STOP the transfusion
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Stopping the transfusion is the universal first step for every reaction.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: A patient develops fever, chills and rigors with a temperature rise of ≥1°C during transfusion, but is otherwise stable. Which reaction is this, and what is the cause?
options: Febrile non-haemolytic — anti-leucocyte antibodies → cytokine release
Minor allergic — reaction to donor plasma proteins
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Febrile non-haemolytic — anti-leucocyte antibodies → cytokine release
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Febrile non-haemolytic reaction is caused by anti-leucocyte antibodies → cytokine release, with fever, chills, rigors (mild, rise ≥1°C); manage by slow/stop, paracetamol, and can restart if stable.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: A patient develops urticaria and pruritus during transfusion with no systemic compromise. What is the management?
options: STOP; IM adrenaline 0.5mg; ABC; IV fluids
STOP immediately; check ID + bag label; Coombs + recross-match
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Stop temporarily; antihistamine; can restart
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: A minor allergic reaction (to donor plasma proteins) causes urticaria and pruritus with no systemic compromise; manage by stopping temporarily, giving an antihistamine, and can restart.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: A patient with IgA deficiency develops hypotension, bronchospasm and angioedema of rapid onset during transfusion. What is the immediate management?
options: STOP; IM adrenaline 0.5mg; ABC; IV fluids
Slow/stop; paracetamol; can restart if stable
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: STOP; IM adrenaline 0.5mg; ABC; IV fluids
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Anaphylaxis (IgA deficiency + anti-IgA antibodies) causes hypotension, bronchospasm, angioedema of rapid onset; manage by STOP, IM adrenaline 0.5mg, ABC, and IV fluids.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: Minutes into a transfusion, a patient develops fever, loin/back pain, hypotension and dark urine. What is the cause, and the immediate action?
options: ABO incompatibility (wrong blood — human error) — STOP immediately; check patient ID + bag label; Coombs + recross-match; supportive
Donor plasma proteins — antihistamine; can restart
Donor antibodies → capillary leak — O₂; NO diuretics
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: ABO incompatibility (wrong blood — human error) — STOP immediately; check patient ID + bag label; Coombs + recross-match; supportive
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Acute haemolytic reaction is due to ABO incompatibility (wrong blood — human error), with fever, loin/back pain, hypotension, dark urine within minutes; STOP immediately, check patient ID + bag label, Coombs + recross-match, and supportive care.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: Within 6h of transfusion a patient develops non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, hypoxia, HYPOtension and fever. Which reaction is this, and how is it managed?
options: TRALI — STOP; O₂ + supportive; NO diuretics
TACO — slow/stop; furosemide + O₂; sit upright
Acute haemolytic — STOP; check ID + bag label
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: TRALI — STOP; O₂ + supportive; NO diuretics
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: TRALI (donor antibodies → neutrophil activation → capillary leak) causes non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, hypoxia, HYPOtension and fever within 6h; manage with STOP, O₂ + supportive, NO diuretics.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: A patient with pre-existing heart failure develops pulmonary oedema, HYPERtension, raised JVP and orthopnoea during transfusion. Which reaction is this, and how is it managed?
options: TACO — slow/stop; furosemide + O₂; sit upright
Acute haemolytic — check ID + bag label
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: TACO — slow/stop; furosemide + O₂; sit upright
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: TACO (volume overload — too fast / pre-existing HF/renal failure) causes pulmonary oedema, HYPERtension, raised JVP and orthopnoea (cardiogenic); manage with slow/stop, furosemide + O₂, and sit upright.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: Both TRALI and TACO cause pulmonary oedema during/after transfusion. What is the key discriminator between them?
options: Blood pressure — TRALI causes hypotension, TACO causes hypertension
Onset — TRALI is always delayed, TACO is immediate
Urine colour — TRALI causes dark urine
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Blood pressure — TRALI causes hypotension, TACO causes hypertension
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Both cause pulmonary oedema; the key difference is blood pressure (and mechanism): TRALI = hypotension, TACO = hypertension.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: How do the oedema mechanisms differ between TRALI and TACO?
options: TRALI = immune-mediated capillary leak (non-cardiogenic); TACO = volume overload (cardiogenic)
TRALI = volume overload (cardiogenic); TACO = capillary leak (non-cardiogenic)
TRALI = ABO incompatibility; TACO = IgA deficiency
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: TRALI = immune-mediated capillary leak (non-cardiogenic); TACO = volume overload (cardiogenic)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: TRALI is immune-mediated capillary leak producing non-cardiogenic oedema; TACO is volume overload producing cardiogenic oedema.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: Which management contrast between TRALI and TACO is correct?
options: TRALI = O₂ + supportive, NO diuretics; TACO = furosemide + O₂
TRALI = furosemide + O₂; TACO = O₂ + supportive, NO diuretics
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: TRALI = O₂ + supportive, NO diuretics; TACO = furosemide + O₂
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: TRALI is managed with O₂ + supportive and NO diuretics; TACO is managed with furosemide + O₂.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: Which memory hook correctly matches the reaction?
options: TRALI — leaky lungs + low BP → no diuretics; TACO — too much fluid + high BP → diurese
TRALI — too much fluid + high BP → diurese; TACO — leaky lungs + low BP → no diuretics
TRALI — ABO mismatch → check ID; TACO — IgA deficiency → adrenaline
TRALI — high BP → furosemide; TACO — low BP → fluids
Both — leaky lungs + low BP → no diuretics
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: TRALI — leaky lungs + low BP → no diuretics; TACO — too much fluid + high BP → diurese
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: The hooks are: TRALI — leaky lungs + low BP → no diuretics; TACO — too much fluid + high BP → diurese.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: In the warfarin reversal sequence, what is the role of FFP?
options: An older alternative; large volume, avoid in fluid overload
Contains factors II, VII, IX, X only
Replaces the need for vitamin K
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: An older alternative; large volume, avoid in fluid overload
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: In the warfarin reversal steps, FFP is an older alternative — large volume, so avoid in fluid overload; PCC is preferred for emergency reversal.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: A 70-year-old man receiving his third unit of blood develops sudden hypotension, loin pain, and dark urine. What is the most likely diagnosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Acute haemolytic transfusion reaction (ABO incompatibility)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Acute haemolytic reactions present with fever, loin pain, haemoglobinuria, and hypotension due to ABO incompatibility causing intravascular haemolysis. Stop transfusion immediately and send the bag + patient sample for cross-match.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: What is TRALI?
options: Non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema within 6h of transfusion due to anti-leukocyte antibodies
Cardiogenic pulmonary oedema from volume overload
Acute haemolytic reaction from ABO incompatibility
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema within 6h of transfusion due to anti-leukocyte antibodies
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: TRALI presents within 6h of transfusion as acute respiratory distress with bilateral infiltrates; PCWP is normal (differentiating from TACO). Anti-HLA or anti-HNA antibodies from donor activate recipient neutrophils.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: Which blood product contains all clotting factors including fibrinogen?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Fresh frozen plasma (FFP)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: FFP contains all clotting factors. Cryoprecipitate is enriched in fibrinogen, factor VIII, vWF, and factor XIII but lacks other factors.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: A patient needs urgent reversal of warfarin before emergency surgery. What is the first-line treatment?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) + vitamin K
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: PCC (Beriplex/Octaplex) provides rapid reversal of warfarin by replenishing factors II, VII, IX, X. IV vitamin K is given concurrently for sustained reversal. FFP takes longer and requires more volume.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: What is the storage temperature and shelf life of platelets?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: 20–24°C with agitation, 5 days
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Platelets are stored at 20–24°C with continuous gentle agitation for up to 5 days. Refrigeration causes platelet activation and reduced function.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: When should irradiated blood products be used?
options: Immunocompromised patients at risk of transfusion-associated GvHD
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Immunocompromised patients at risk of transfusion-associated GvHD
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Irradiated products destroy donor T-lymphocytes and are used in patients with severe immunocompromise (SCT, haematological malignancy, congenital immunodeficiency) to prevent TA-GvHD, which is fatal.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: What is the Hb threshold for red cell transfusion in a stable, asymptomatic adult without cardiac disease?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Hb <70 g/L
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: NICE/BSH guidelines: transfuse at Hb <70 g/L in stable patients. Target 70–90 g/L post-transfusion. Cardiac patients may have a higher threshold of <80 g/L.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: What is cryoprecipitate particularly rich in?
options: Fibrinogen, factor VIII, vWF, factor XIII
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Fibrinogen, factor VIII, vWF, factor XIII
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Cryoprecipitate is the cold-precipitate from FFP, concentrated in fibrinogen (most important), factor VIII, vWF, and factor XIII. It is used for hypofibrinogenaemia in DIC and massive haemorrhage.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: A patient develops fever, chills, and mild urticaria 30 minutes into a blood transfusion but no haemodynamic compromise or respiratory distress. What is the most likely reaction?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Febrile non-haemolytic transfusion reaction
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Febrile non-haemolytic reactions are the most common transfusion reaction, caused by cytokines in stored blood or anti-leukocyte antibodies. Mild fever/chills without haemolysis or respiratory compromise. Slow transfusion rate and give paracetamol.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.question: EXAM PEARL: What is the complication of repeated red cell transfusions in haemoglobinopathies?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.answer: Iron overload requiring chelation therapy
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Blood Transfusi.explanation: Repeated transfusions in thalassaemia/sickle cell disease cause iron overload (haemosiderosis) — each unit delivers ~250 mg iron. Chelation with desferrioxamine (IV/SC) or deferasirox (oral) is required.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: What is the clinical significance and typical timing of neutropenic sepsis?
options: A medical emergency — the commonest serious complication of chemotherapy, typically 7–14 days post-cycle (the nadir)
A chronic complication seen months after chemotherapy
A reaction seen during the chemotherapy infusion itself
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: A medical emergency — the commonest serious complication of chemotherapy, typically 7–14 days post-cycle (the nadir)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: Neutropenic sepsis is a medical emergency and the commonest serious complication of chemotherapy, typically occurring 7–14 days post-cycle (the nadir).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: What is the definition of neutropenic sepsis?
options: Neutrophils <0.5 ×10⁹/L on anticancer treatment PLUS temp >38°C or clinical signs of sepsis
Any fever in a cancer patient
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Neutrophils <0.5 ×10⁹/L on anticancer treatment PLUS temp >38°C or clinical signs of sepsis
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: Neutropenic sepsis is defined as neutrophils <0.5 ×10⁹/L in a patient on anticancer treatment PLUS either temp >38°C or clinical signs of sepsis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: Why are the signs of neutropenic sepsis often blunted?
options: Without neutrophils there is less inflammatory response, so fever may be the only sign
Because the infection is always viral
Because the count is too high to react
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Without neutrophils there is less inflammatory response, so fever may be the only sign
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: Without neutrophils there is less inflammatory response, so fever may be the only sign; the patient may be hypothermic, confused, or hypotensive instead — maintain a low threshold to treat.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: A chemotherapy patient at day 10 post-cycle is hypothermic and confused with no fever. What should you do?
options: Treat as neutropenic sepsis — maintain a low threshold, as signs may be blunted
Wait for a documented fever before treating
Only treat if cultures return positive
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Treat as neutropenic sepsis — maintain a low threshold, as signs may be blunted
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: Signs may be blunted — without neutrophils, a patient may be hypothermic, confused, or hypotensive rather than febrile; maintain a low threshold to treat.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: What is the commonest organism in neutropenic sepsis, and its usual source?
options: Staph epidermidis (coagulase-negative Gram-positive) — usually from indwelling lines
E. coli — from the urinary tract
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Staph epidermidis (coagulase-negative Gram-positive) — usually from indwelling lines
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: The commonest organism is Staph epidermidis (coagulase-negative Gram-positive), usually from indwelling lines in cancer patients.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: Why is piperacillin-tazobactam (Tazocin) chosen over narrow Gram-positive cover?
options: Empirical cover must target Gram-negatives including Pseudomonas
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Empirical cover must target Gram-negatives including Pseudomonas
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: Empirical cover must target Gram-negatives including Pseudomonas, which is why Tazocin is chosen over narrow Gram-positive cover.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: What is the key principle of the emergency response in neutropenic sepsis?
options: Antibiotics are NOT delayed for investigations — give Tazocin first, take cultures around it
Always await blood cultures before antibiotics
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Antibiotics are NOT delayed for investigations — give Tazocin first, take cultures around it
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: Antibiotics are not delayed for investigations — give Tazocin first and take cultures around it.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: What is the first action in the emergency response, and within what timeframe?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: IV piperacillin-tazobactam (Tazocin) immediately — within 1 hour ('door-to-needle')
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: Step 1 is IV piperacillin-tazobactam (Tazocin) immediately — within 1 hour ('door-to-needle'), before cultures if needed.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: Which investigations make up the cultures + septic screen (Step 2)?
options: Blood (peripheral and line), FBC, CRP, U&E, LFT, clotting, lactate; CXR, urine/sputum/stool
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Blood (peripheral and line), FBC, CRP, U&E, LFT, clotting, lactate; CXR, urine/sputum/stool
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: Step 2 is cultures + septic screen: blood (peripheral and line), FBC, CRP, U&E, LFT, clotting, lactate, plus CXR and urine/sputum/stool.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: A neutropenic sepsis patient remains febrile and unwell at 48 hours on Tazocin. What is the next step?
options: Escalate to meropenem ± vancomycin (vancomycin if line infection/MRSA suspected)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Escalate to meropenem ± vancomycin (vancomycin if line infection/MRSA suspected)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: If still febrile/unwell at 48h, escalate to meropenem ± vancomycin (vancomycin if line infection/MRSA suspected).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: When is vancomycin added during escalation?
options: If line infection / MRSA is suspected
Only if fungal infection is found
Only if the patient is apyrexial
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: If line infection / MRSA is suspected
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: Vancomycin is added (to meropenem at the 48h escalation) if a line infection or MRSA is suspected.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: A neutropenic sepsis patient remains unresponsive to antibiotics at 4–6 days. What should be done?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Investigate fungal infection → antifungals (e.g. amphotericin)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: At 4–6 days unresponsive, investigate fungal infection and start antifungals (e.g. amphotericin).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: What is the de-escalation strategy in neutropenic sepsis?
options: Switch to oral antibiotics once apyrexial for 48h; continue 10–14 days total
Stop antibiotics as soon as the first dose is given
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Switch to oral antibiotics once apyrexial for 48h; continue 10–14 days total
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: De-escalation: switch to oral antibiotics once apyrexial for 48h, and continue 10–14 days total.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: What prophylaxis is given when neutrophils are anticipated to fall <0.5?
options: Fluoroquinolone prophylaxis (e.g. ciprofloxacin) during the expected nadir
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Fluoroquinolone prophylaxis (e.g. ciprofloxacin) during the expected nadir
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: When anticipated neutrophils <0.5, fluoroquinolone prophylaxis (e.g. ciprofloxacin) is given during the expected nadir.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: What is the role of G-CSF (filgrastim) in prophylaxis?
options: Shortens the duration of neutropenia in high-risk chemotherapy regimens
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Shortens the duration of neutropenia in high-risk chemotherapy regimens
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: G-CSF (filgrastim) shortens the duration of neutropenia in high-risk chemotherapy regimens.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: EXAM PEARL: How is the diagnosis of neutropenic sepsis best summarised?
options: Neutrophils <0.5 + temp >38°C (or sepsis signs) on chemo = neutropenic sepsis — the definition is the diagnosis
It requires clinical judgement beyond the criteria
It needs a positive blood culture first
It is diagnosed only by the oncology team
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Neutrophils <0.5 + temp >38°C (or sepsis signs) on chemo = neutropenic sepsis — the definition is the diagnosis
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: Neutrophils <0.5 + temp >38°C (or sepsis signs) on chemo = neutropenic sepsis — the definition is the diagnosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: EXAM PEARL: What is the rule about Tazocin timing?
options: Tazocin within 1 hour — do NOT wait for cultures or imaging
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Tazocin within 1 hour — do NOT wait for cultures or imaging
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: Give Tazocin within 1 hour — do NOT wait for cultures or imaging.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: EXAM PEARL: What is the escalation ladder in neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Tazocin → meropenem ± vancomycin (48h) → antifungals (4–6 days)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: The escalation ladder is Tazocin → meropenem ± vancomycin (48h) → antifungals (4–6 days).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: EXAM PEARL: What is the commonest organism versus what empirical cover targets?
options: Commonest organism: Staph epidermidis (lines); empirical cover targets Pseudomonas/Gram-negatives
Commonest organism: Pseudomonas; cover targets Staph epidermidis
Commonest organism: Candida; cover targets Gram-positives
Commonest organism: E. coli; cover targets fungi
Commonest organism: MRSA; cover targets viruses
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Commonest organism: Staph epidermidis (lines); empirical cover targets Pseudomonas/Gram-negatives
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: The commonest organism is Staph epidermidis (from lines), but empirical cover targets Pseudomonas/Gram-negatives.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: EXAM PEARL: What is the prophylaxis, and which complications does the note cross-reference?
options: Fluoroquinolone ± G-CSF; cross-ref chemo complications (TLS, marrow failure)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Fluoroquinolone ± G-CSF; cross-ref chemo complications (TLS, marrow failure)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: Prophylaxis is fluoroquinolone ± G-CSF; the note cross-references chemo complications (tumour lysis syndrome, marrow failure).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: A patient on chemotherapy presents with a temperature of 38.5°C and neutrophils of 0.3 ×10⁹/L. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Neutropenic sepsis
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: Neutrophils <0.5 ×10⁹/L (here 0.3) on anticancer treatment with temp >38°C meets the definition of neutropenic sepsis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: Within what timeframe must the first dose of antibiotics be given in neutropenic sepsis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Within 1 hour
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: The 'door-to-needle' target is to give IV Tazocin within 1 hour, before cultures if needed.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: Which best describes the inflammatory response in neutropenic sepsis?
options: Muted — fewer neutrophils mean less inflammation, so fever may be the only sign
Exaggerated — florid inflammation is always present
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Muted — fewer neutrophils mean less inflammation, so fever may be the only sign
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: The inflammatory response is muted because there are fewer neutrophils, so fever may be the only sign and hypothermia/confusion/hypotension may occur instead.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: What should be done with antibiotics relative to taking cultures in suspected neutropenic sepsis?
options: Give Tazocin first and take cultures around it — do not delay antibiotics
Take all cultures and wait for results before antibiotics
Withhold antibiotics until imaging is done
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Give Tazocin first and take cultures around it — do not delay antibiotics
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: Antibiotics are not delayed for investigations — give Tazocin first and take cultures around it.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: Which agent is used if fungal infection is suspected after 4–6 days of unresponsiveness?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Amphotericin
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: If fungal infection is suspected at 4–6 days, antifungals such as amphotericin are used.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: When are oral antibiotics appropriate in neutropenic sepsis?
options: Once apyrexial for 48h, continuing 10–14 days total
Only after 6 weeks of IV therapy
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Once apyrexial for 48h, continuing 10–14 days total
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: De-escalation to oral antibiotics is appropriate once apyrexial for 48h, continuing 10–14 days total.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: Why is neutropenic sepsis described as 'a definition, not a judgement call'?
options: If the neutrophil and temperature/sepsis criteria are met on anticancer treatment, the diagnosis is made
Because only seniors can diagnose it
Because it requires a scoring system
Because it depends on culture results
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: If the neutrophil and temperature/sepsis criteria are met on anticancer treatment, the diagnosis is made
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: The diagnosis is a definition, not a judgement call: meeting the neutrophil and temperature/sepsis-sign criteria in a patient on anticancer treatment makes the diagnosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: Which combination of antibiotics is the escalation choice at 48h if the patient remains unwell?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Meropenem ± vancomycin
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: At 48h, the escalation is to meropenem ± vancomycin (vancomycin if line infection/MRSA is suspected).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: Which prophylactic measure shortens neutropenia duration rather than preventing infection directly?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: G-CSF (filgrastim)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: G-CSF (filgrastim) shortens the duration of neutropenia in high-risk chemotherapy regimens, whereas fluoroquinolone prophylaxis targets infection during the nadir.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: From which source does the commonest organism in neutropenic sepsis typically arise?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Indwelling lines
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: Staph epidermidis, the commonest organism, usually arises from indwelling lines in cancer patients.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: A 45-year-old woman on CHOP chemotherapy for DLBCL presents on day 10 with temperature 38.8°C. Her neutrophil count is 0.2 × 10⁹/L. What is the immediate management?
options: IV piperacillin/tazobactam within 1 hour after blood cultures
Oral ciprofloxacin and send home if stable
Wait for culture results before starting antibiotics
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: IV piperacillin/tazobactam within 1 hour after blood cultures
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: Neutropenic sepsis is a haematological emergency. Blood cultures should be taken (peripheral ± central line) then IV piperacillin/tazobactam started within 1 hour. Do not wait for culture results.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: Which organism is the most feared in neutropenic sepsis due to its rapid fatality?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: Pseudomonas aeruginosa causes fulminant, rapidly fatal sepsis in neutropenic patients. Its intrinsic antibiotic resistance and endotoxin make it particularly deadly. Piperacillin/tazobactam and meropenem provide Pseudomonas cover.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: After 5 days of IV antibiotics a neutropenic patient remains febrile with neutrophil count 0.1 × 10⁹/L. What should be added?
options: Antifungal therapy (caspofungin or voriconazole) and CT chest for Aspergillus
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Antifungal therapy (caspofungin or voriconazole) and CT chest for Aspergillus
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: Persistent fever after 4–7 days of antibiotics in prolonged neutropenia should prompt empirical antifungal therapy (caspofungin for Candida/Aspergillus, voriconazole if Aspergillus suspected). CT chest looks for the 'halo sign' of invasive pulmonary aspergillosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: What is the 'halo sign' on CT chest and what does it suggest?
options: Ground-glass halo surrounding a pulmonary nodule — suggests invasive pulmonary aspergillosis
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Ground-glass halo surrounding a pulmonary nodule — suggests invasive pulmonary aspergillosis
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: The 'halo sign' (CT ground-glass opacity surrounding a nodule) represents haemorrhagic infarction around angio-invasive Aspergillus. Seen in immunocompromised patients with neutropenia. Treat with voriconazole IV.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: Which patient group should receive co-trimoxazole (PCP) prophylaxis?
options: ALL patients on treatment, stem cell transplant recipients, and patients on prolonged high-dose corticosteroids
Only those with prior PCP infection
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: ALL patients on treatment, stem cell transplant recipients, and patients on prolonged high-dose corticosteroids
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: PCP prophylaxis with co-trimoxazole (or dapsone if sulfa-allergic) is given to ALL patients, SCT recipients, and those on prolonged high-dose steroids (>20 mg prednisolone >4 weeks) — risk of Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia is high in these groups.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: When is G-CSF (filgrastim) prophylaxis recommended in chemotherapy?
options: When febrile neutropenia risk is >20% with the chemotherapy regimen
Only after a proven neutropenic sepsis episode
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: When febrile neutropenia risk is >20% with the chemotherapy regimen
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: ASCO/NICE recommend G-CSF prophylaxis when the febrile neutropenia risk is >20% with the planned regimen (e.g. BEACOPP, dose-dense chemotherapy). It significantly reduces neutropenic sepsis episodes and hospitalisation.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: What should be done with a central venous line in a neutropenic patient with confirmed Candida fungaemia?
options: Leave the line in if patient is stable
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Remove the line immediately
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: Candidaemia mandates immediate line removal (source control) regardless of patient stability. Central lines are a nidus for persistent Candida biofilm. Treat with micafungin, caspofungin, or fluconazole (if fluconazole-sensitive).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: What is the MASCC score used for in neutropenic sepsis?
options: Identify low-risk patients suitable for oral antibiotics/early discharge
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Identify low-risk patients suitable for oral antibiotics/early discharge
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: MASCC score ≥21 identifies low-risk febrile neutropenia — these patients can be managed with oral antibiotics (ciprofloxacin + co-amoxiclav) and early discharge. Score <21 = high risk requiring IV antibiotics and inpatient care.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: A neutropenic patient develops right iliac fossa pain, diarrhoea, and fever. CT shows thickening of the caecum. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Neutropenic enterocolitis (typhlitis)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: Neutropenic enterocolitis (typhlitis) is a life-threatening complication of profound neutropenia — bowel wall invasion by bacteria/fungi → ischaemia/necrosis, predominantly affecting the caecum. CT shows caecal wall thickening. Treat with IV antibiotics; surgery if perforation/necrosis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.question: EXAM PEARL: What is the antibiotic time target in neutropenic sepsis?
options: Antibiotics within 1 hour of presentation — do not wait for culture results
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.answer: Antibiotics within 1 hour of presentation — do not wait for culture results
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__Neutropenic Sep.explanation: NICE guidelines: IV antibiotics (piperacillin/tazobactam) must be given within 1 hour of presentation in neutropenic sepsis. Blood cultures should be taken beforehand if possible, but should not delay antibiotics by more than minutes.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.question: What is the decisive mechanism (the fork) in DIC?
options: Consumption — massive coagulation activation consumes platelets and clotting factors faster than they are replaced
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.answer: Consumption — massive coagulation activation consumes platelets and clotting factors faster than they are replaced
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.explanation: The decisive fork in DIC is consumption: massive coagulation activation consumes platelets and clotting factors faster than they are replaced, giving simultaneous clotting and bleeding.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.question: Is DIC ever a primary condition?
options: No — DIC is always secondary to an underlying trigger
Yes — primary DIC is the commonest form
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.answer: No — DIC is always secondary to an underlying trigger
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.explanation: DIC is always secondary — there is no primary DIC.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.question: What is the core paradox of DIC?
options: Too much clotting and too little clotting simultaneously — microvascular thrombosis plus haemorrhage
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.answer: Too much clotting and too little clotting simultaneously — microvascular thrombosis plus haemorrhage
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.explanation: The core paradox is too much clotting and too little clotting simultaneously — microvascular thrombosis plus haemorrhage.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.question: How do FDPs contribute to bleeding in DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.answer: They inhibit fibrin polymerisation
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.explanation: In the mechanism chain, secondary fibrinolysis produces FDPs, which themselves worsen bleeding by inhibiting fibrin polymerisation.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.question: What is the unifying mechanism behind all DIC triggers?
options: Anything that exposes or expresses tissue factor
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.answer: Anything that exposes or expresses tissue factor
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.explanation: The unifying mechanism is anything that exposes or expresses tissue factor — endothelial damage, monocyte TF expression driven by cytokines, or direct TF release.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.question: What is the commonest cause of DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.answer: Sepsis (especially Gram-negative)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.explanation: Sepsis (especially Gram-negative) is the commonest cause, via cytokine-driven TF expression on monocytes.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.question: Which obstetric causes can trigger DIC?
options: Amniotic fluid embolism, HELLP syndrome, placental abruption, retained products of conception
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.answer: Amniotic fluid embolism, HELLP syndrome, placental abruption, retained products of conception
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.explanation: Obstetric triggers of DIC include amniotic fluid embolism, HELLP syndrome, placental abruption, and retained products of conception.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.question: Which leukaemia is the classic haematological trigger for DIC, and why?
options: AML M0 — Auer rods activate platelets
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.answer: APML — promyelocytes release procoagulant granules
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.explanation: Acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APML) is the classic leukaemia trigger; promyelocytes release procoagulant granules, and ATRA treatment itself initially worsens DIC.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.question: Treatment of which condition itself initially worsens DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.answer: APML (with ATRA)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.explanation: Treatment of APML with ATRA itself initially worsens DIC.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.question: What is the exam buzzword for the bleeding end of DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.answer: Oozing from ≥3 unrelated sites
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.explanation: Oozing from ≥3 unrelated sites is the exam buzzword for the haemorrhagic end of DIC.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.question: Which is a thrombotic (thrombotic end) feature of DIC?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.answer: Purpura fulminans (digital/skin necrosis)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.explanation: Thrombotic features include microvascular occlusion → end-organ ischaemia, AKI (renal cortical necrosis), delirium/reduced GCS, purpura fulminans (digital/skin necrosis), and respiratory failure (ARDS pattern).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.question: What happens to platelets and PT/APTT/TT in DIC, and why?
options: Platelets low (consumed in microthrombi); PT/APTT/TT prolonged (clotting factors consumed)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.answer: Platelets low (consumed in microthrombi); PT/APTT/TT prolonged (clotting factors consumed)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.explanation: Platelets are low (consumed in microthrombi) and PT/APTT/TT are all prolonged (clotting factors consumed).

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.question: What happens to D-dimer/FDPs in DIC, and why?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.answer: Markedly raised — secondary fibrinolysis
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.explanation: D-dimer/FDPs are markedly raised in DIC due to secondary fibrinolysis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.question: Why might fibrinogen be normal early in DIC?
options: It is an acute phase reactant
It is not consumed in DIC
It is replaced by the spleen
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.answer: It is an acute phase reactant
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.explanation: Fibrinogen is consumed but, being an acute phase reactant, may be normal early in DIC.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.question: What does the blood film show in DIC, and why?
options: Schistocytes — RBCs sheared through fibrin strands in vessels
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.answer: Schistocytes — RBCs sheared through fibrin strands in vessels
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.explanation: The blood film shows schistocytes (fragmented RBCs) sheared through fibrin strands in vessels.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.question: A septic patient oozes from three cannula sites; bloods show low platelets, prolonged PT/APTT, low fibrinogen, very high D-dimer and schistocytes. What is the diagnosis?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.answer: DIC
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.explanation: Low platelets, raised PT/APTT, low fibrinogen, raised D-dimer, and schistocytes together = DIC until proven otherwise, here triggered by sepsis.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.question: What is the key discriminator (Factor VIII) between DIC and liver disease?
options: Factor VIII is normal/high in liver disease but low in DIC
Factor VIII is low in liver disease but high in DIC
Factor VIII is normal in both
Factor VIII is low in both
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.answer: Factor VIII is normal/high in liver disease but low in DIC
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.explanation: Factor VIII is extrahepatic — normal/high in liver disease but low in DIC; this is the key discriminator.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.question: On the discriminator table, what is the coagulation screen in TTP/HUS?
options: Normal PT/APTT and fibrinogen, with schistocytes present
Low fibrinogen with low Factor VIII
Markedly raised D-dimer with deranged PT
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.answer: Normal PT/APTT and fibrinogen, with schistocytes present
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.explanation: In TTP/HUS, PT/APTT and fibrinogen are normal and Factor VIII is normal, yet schistocytes are present — thrombocytopenia + schistocytes with a normal coagulation screen.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.question: On the discriminator table, are schistocytes present in liver disease?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.answer: No
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.explanation: Schistocytes are present in DIC and TTP/HUS but not in liver disease.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.question: What is Priority 1 in managing DIC?
options: Treat the underlying cause — the only thing that reverses DIC
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.answer: Treat the underlying cause — the only thing that reverses DIC
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.explanation: Priority 1 is treating the underlying cause (antibiotics for sepsis, delivery in obstetric cases, treat APML) — the only thing that reverses DIC; everything else is supportive.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.question: In DIC, when are blood products such as platelets and FFP given?
options: Only if the patient is afebrile
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.answer: Only if bleeding or pre-procedure
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.explanation: Supportive products (platelets, FFP, cryoprecipitate, red cells) are given only if bleeding or pre-procedure — treat the patient, not the numbers alone.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.question: What does cryoprecipitate replace in DIC, and to what target?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.answer: Fibrinogen — target >1.5 g/L
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.explanation: Cryoprecipitate replaces fibrinogen, with a target >1.5 g/L; FFP replaces all clotting factors and platelets are kept >50 ×10⁹/L if bleeding.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.question: When is heparin considered in DIC?
options: Only in thrombosis-predominant DIC (e.g. purpura fulminans)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.answer: Only in thrombosis-predominant DIC (e.g. purpura fulminans)
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.explanation: Heparin is considered only in thrombosis-predominant DIC (e.g. purpura fulminans) and is generally avoided when bleeding dominates — a common distractor.

conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.question: A patient with DIC has dominant microvascular clotting (purpura fulminans) with minimal bleeding. What may be considered?
conditions__HAEMATOLOGY__DIC (Disseminat.answer: Heparin
